=Conjunctions=
{{image|chapter-connectives-picture|The picture for chapter 14|CLL-chapter-connectives.gif}}
{{ssp|section-connectives-introduction}}
==Logical connection and truth tables==

{{ind|general-imported|truth functions}}  {{ind|general-imported|logical language|truth functions}} Lojban is a logical language: the name of the language itself means 

“logical language”. The fundamentals of ordinary logic (there are variant logics, which aren't addressed in this book) include the notions of a “sentence” (sometimes called a “statement” or “proposition”), which asserts a truth or falsehood, and a small set of “truth functions”, which combine two sentences to create a new sentence. The truth functions have the special characteristic that the truth value (that is, the truth or falsehood) of the results depends only on the truth value of the component sentences. For example,

{{dsp|example-random-id-mJ6y}}
{{judri|c14e1d1}}
{{ind|example|man or woman|example}}
John is a man or James is a woman.

is true if 
“John is a man” is true, or if 
“James is a woman” is true. If we know whether John is a man, and we know whether James is a woman, we know whether 
“John is a man or James is a woman” is true, provided we know the meaning of 
“or”. Here 
“John is a man” and 
“James is a woman” are the component sentences.

{{ind|general-imported|negating a sentence|and truth value}} We will use the phrase “negating a sentence” to mean changing its truth value. An English sentence may always be negated by prefixing 

“It is false that ...”, or more idiomatically by inserting 
“not” at the right point, generally before the verb. 
“James is not a woman” is the negation of 
“James is a woman”, and vice versa. Recent slang can also negate a sentence by following it with the exclamation 
“Not!”

{{ind|general-imported|logical connectives}} Words like 
“or” are called “logical connectives”, and Lojban has many of them, as befits a logical language. This chapter is mostly concerned with explaining the forms and uses of the Lojban logical connectives. There are a number of other logical connectives in English such as “and”, “and/or”, “if”, “only if”, “whether or not”, and others; however, not every use of these English words corresponds to a logical connective. This point will be made clear in particular cases as needed. The other English meanings are supported by different Lojban connective constructs.

The Lojban connectives form a system (as the title of this chapter suggests), regular and predictable, whereas natural-language connectives are rather less systematic and therefore less predictable.

{{ind|general-imported|truth table|explanation}}  {{ind|general-imported|truth functions|16 possible}} There exist 16 possible different truth functions. A truth table is a graphical device for specifying a truth function, making it clear what the value of the truth function is for every possible value of the component sentences. Here is a truth table for 

“or”:

<tab class=wikitable header=true>
first	second	result
True	True	True
True	False	True
False	True	True
False	False	False
</tab>
This table means that if the first sentence stated is true, and the second sentence stated is true, then the result of the truth function is also true. The same is true for every other possible combination of truth values except the one where both the first and the second sentences are false, in which case the truth value of the result is also false.

Suppose that 
“John is a man” is true (and 
“John is not a man” is false), and that 
“James is a woman” is false (and 
“James is not a woman” is true). Then the truth table tells us that

:''“John is a man, or James is not a woman”             (true   true )  is true''
:''“John is a man, or James is a woman”                 (true , false)  is true''
:''“John is not a man, or James is not a woman”         (false, true )  is true''
:''“John is not a man, or James is a woman”             (false, false)  is false''

{{ind|general-imported|&quot;or&quot;|&quot;and/or&quot; contrasted with &quot;either … or … but not both&quot;}} Note that the kind of 
“or” used in this example can also be expressed (in formal English) with 
“and/or”. There is a different truth table for the kind of “or” that means “either ... or ... but not both”.

{{ind|general-imported|truth tables|notation convention}}  {{ind|general-imported|truth tables|abbreviated format}} To save space, we will write truth tables in a shorter format henceforth. Let the letters T and F stand for True and False. The rows will always be given in the order shown above: TT, TF, FT, FF for the two sentences. Then it is only necessary to give the four letters from the result column, which can be written TTTF, as can be seen by reading down the third column of the table above. So TTTF is the abbreviated truth table for the 

“or” truth function. Here are the 16 possible truth functions, with an English version of what it means to assert that each function is, in fact, true ( 
“first” refers to the first sentence, and 
“second” to the second sentence):

{{ind|general-imported|truth tables|list of 16 in abbreviated form}}
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
TTTT	(always true)
TTTF	first is true and/or second is true.
TTFT	first is true if second is true.
TTFF	first is true whether or not second is true.
TFTT	first is true only if second is true.
TFTF	whether or not first is true, second is true.
TFFT	first is true if and only if second is true.
TFFF	first is true and second is true
FTTT	first and second are not both true.
FTTF	first or second is true, but not both.
FTFT	whether or not first is true, second is false.
FTFF	first is true, but second is false.
FFTT	first is false whether or not second is true.
FFTF	first is false, but second is true.
FFFT	neither first nor second is true.
FFFF	(always false)
</tab>
Skeptics may work out the detailed truth tables for themselves.

{{ssp|section-four-basics}}
==The Four basic vowels==
{{ind|general-imported|logical connectives|relation to truth functions}}  {{ind|general-imported|truth functions|relation to logical connectives}}  {{ind|general-imported|truth functions|fundamental 4 in Lojban}} Lojban regards four of these 16 truth functions as fundamental, and assigns them the four vowels A, E, O, and U. These letters do not represent actual cmavo or selma'o, but rather a component vowel from which actual logical-connective cmavo are built up, as explained in the next section. Here are the four vowels, their truth tables, and rough English equivalents:

{{ind|general-imported|fancy U|notation convention}}  {{ind|general-imported|fancy O|notation convention}}  {{ind|general-imported|fancy E|notation convention}}  {{ind|general-imported|fancy A|notation convention}}  {{ind|general-imported|truth tables|for 4 fundamental Lojban truth functions}}
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
A	TTTF	or, and/or
E	TFFF	and
O	TFFT	if and only if
U	TTFF	whether or not
</tab>
More precisely:

:'''A is true if either or both sentences are true'''
:'''E is true if both sentences are true, but not otherwise'''
:'''O is true if the sentences are both true or both false'''
:'''U is true if the first sentence is true, regardless of the truth value of the second sentence'''

{{ind|general-imported|truth functions|creating all 16 with Lojban's basic set}} With the four vowels, the ability to negate either sentence, and the ability to exchange the sentences, as if their order had been reversed, we can create all of the 16 possible truth functions except TTTT and FFFF, which are fairly useless anyway. The following table illustrates how to create each of the 14 remaining truth functions:

<tab class=wikitable header=true>
TTTF	A
TTFT	A with second sentence negated
TTFF	U
TFTT	A with first sentence negated
TFTF	U with sentences exchanged
TFFT	O
TFFF	E
FTTT	A with both sentences negated
FTTF	O with either first or second negated (not both)
FTFT	U with sentences exchanged and then second negated
FTFF	E with second sentence negated
FFTT	U with first sentence negated
FFTF	E with first sentence negated
FFFT	E with both sentences negated
</tab>
{{ind|general-imported|truth functions|commutative}}  {{ind|general-imported|commutative truth functions}} Note that exchanging the sentences is only necessary with U. The three other basic truth functions are commutative; that is, they mean the same thing regardless of the order of the component sentences. There are other ways of getting some of these truth tables; these just happen to be the methods usually employed.

{{ssp|section-six-types}}
==The six types of logical connectives==
{{ind|general-imported|logical connectives|rationale for multiple sets in grammar}} In order to remain unambiguous, Lojban cannot have only a single logical connective for each truth function. There are many places in the grammar of the language where logical connection is permitted, and each must have its appropriate set of connectives. If the connective suitable for sumti were used to connect selbri, ambiguity would result.

Consider the English sentence:

{{dsp|example-random-id-ptgf}}
{{judri|c14e3d1}}
{{ind|example|window|example}}
Mary went to the window and ...

where the last word could be followed by 
“the door”, a noun phrase, or by 
“saw the horses”, a sentence with subject omitted, or by 
“John went to the door”, a full sentence, or by one of a variety of other English grammatical constructions. Lojban cannot tolerate such grammatical looseness.

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|JA selma'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|logical connectives|selma'o|enumerated}} Instead, there are a total of five different selma'o used for logical connection: A, GA, GIhA, GUhA, and JA. Each of these includes four cmavo, one based on each of the four vowels, which is always the last vowel in the cmavo. In selma'o A, the vowel is the entire cmavo.

{{ind|general-imported|logical connectives|cmavo|format for each selma'o}} Thus, in selma'o A, the cmavo for the function A is {{vla|a}}. (Do not confuse A, which is a selma'o, with A, which is a truth function, or {{vla|a}}, which is a cmavo.) Likewise, the cmavo for E in selma'o GIhA is {{vla|gi'e}}, and the cmavo for U in selma'o GA is {{vla|gu}}. This systematic regularity makes the cmavo easier to learn.

{{ind|general-imported|compound logical connectives|components}} Obviously, four cmavo are not enough to express the 14 truth functions explained in 
{{ls|section-connectives-introduction}}. Therefore, compound cmavo must be used. These compound cmavo follow a systematic pattern: each has one cmavo from the five logical connection selma'o at its heart, and may also contain one or more of the auxiliary cmavo 
{{vla|se}}, 
{{vla|na}}, or 
{{vla|nai}}. Which auxiliaries are used with which logical connection cmavo, and with what grammar and meaning, will be explained in the following sections. The uses of each of these auxiliary cmavo relates to its other uses in other parts of Lojban grammar.

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|JA selma'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|jek|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|ek|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|-ek|in name for logical connectives}}  {{ind|general-imported|compound logical connectives|naming convention}} For convenience, each of the types of compound cmavo used for logical connection is designated by a Lojban name. The name is derived by changing the final 
“-A” of the selma'o name to 
“-ek”; the reasons for using 
“-ek” are buried deep in the history of the Loglan Project. Thus, compound cmavo based on selma'o A are known as eks, and those based on selma'o JA are known as jeks. (When writing in English, it is conventional to use 
“eks” as the plural of “ek”.) When the term “logical connective” is used in this chapter, it refers to one or more of these kinds of compound cmavo.

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|JA selma'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|ijek|definition}} Why does the title of this section refer to 
“six types” when there are only five selma'o? A jek may be preceded by 
{{vla|i}}, the usual Lojban cmavo for connecting two sentences. The compound produced by 
{{vla|i}} followed by a jek is known as an ijek. It is useful to think of ijeks as a sixth kind of logical connective, parallel to eks, jeks, geks, giheks, and guheks.

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|JOI selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|GI selma'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|ijoik|as name for compound cmavo}}  {{ind|general-imported|joigik|as name for compound cmavo}}  {{ind|general-imported|joik|as name for compound cmavo}}  {{ind|general-imported|gik|as name for compound cmavo}} There also exist giks, joiks, ijoiks, and joigiks, which are not logical connectives, but are other kinds of compound cmavo which will be introduced later.

{{ssp|section-bridi-connection}}
==Logical connection of bridi==
{{ind|general-imported|bridi|logical connective for}}  {{ind|general-imported|ijek logical connectives|connecting bridi}} Now we are ready to express 
{{lex|example-random-id-mJ6y}} in Lojban! The kind of logical connective which is placed between two Lojban bridi to connect them logically is an ijek:

{{dsp|example-random-id-h2hN}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-h2hN}}
{{judri|c14e4d1}}
:'''la djan. nanmu .ija la djeimyz. ninmu'''
:<code>John is-a-man or James is-a-woman.</code>

Here we have two separate Lojban bridi, {{jbo|la djan. nanmu}} and {{jbo|la djeimyz. ninmu}}. These bridi are connected by {{vla|.i}}{{vla|ja}}, the ijek for the truth function A. The {{vla|i}} portion of the ijek tells us that we are dealing with separate sentences here. Similarly, we can now say:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qGiu}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qGiu}}
{{judri|c14e4d2}}
:'''la djan. nanmu .ije la djeimyz. ninmu'''
:<code>John is-a-man and James is-a-woman.</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qGIu}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qGIu}}
{{judri|c14e4d3}}
:'''la djan. nanmu .ijo la djeimyz. ninmu'''
:<code>John is-a-man if-and-only-if James is-a-woman.</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qgJC}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qgJC}}
{{judri|c14e4d4}}
:'''la djan. nanmu .iju la djeimyz. ninmu'''
:<code>John is-a-man whether-or-not James is-a-woman.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|bridi|logical connection with negation}} To obtain the other truth tables listed in 

{{ls|section-four-basics}}, we need to know how to negate the two bridi which represent the component sentences. We could negate them directly by inserting 
{{vla|na}} before the selbri, but Lojban also allows us to place the negation within the connective itself.

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|JA selma'o}} To negate the first or left-hand bridi, prefix 
{{vla|na}} to the JA cmavo but after the 
{{vla|i}}. To negate the second or right-hand bridi, suffix 
:{{jbo|-nai}} to the JA cmavo. In either case, the negating word is placed on the side of the connective that is closest to the bridi being negated.

So to express the truth table FTTF, which requires O with either of the two bridi negated (not both), we can say either:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qgKB}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qgKB}}
{{judri|c14e4d5}}
:'''la djan. nanmu .inajo la djeimyz. ninmu'''
:<code>John is-not-a-man if-and-only-if James is-a-woman.</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qgLH}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qgLH}}
{{judri|c14e4d6}}
:'''la djan. nanmu .ijonai la djeimyz. ninmu'''
:<code>John is a man if-and-only-if James is-not-a-woman</code>

The meaning of both 
{{lex|example-random-id-qgKB}} and 
{{lex|example-random-id-qgLH}} is the same as that of:

{{dsp|example-random-id-1Kp9}}
{{judri|c14e4d7}}
John is a man or James is a woman, but not both.

Here is another example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-FXSC}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-FXSC}}
{{judri|c14e4d8}}
:'''la djan. nanmu .ijanai la djeimyz. ninmu'''
:<code>John is-a-man or James is-not-a-woman.</code>
:''John is a man if James is a woman.''

{{ind|general-imported|if|English usage contrasted with Lojban logical connective}}  {{ind|general-imported|if|meaning in logical connections}} How's that again? Are those two English sentences in 
{{lex|example-random-id-FXSC}} really equivalent? In English, no. The Lojban TTFT truth function can be glossed 
“A if B”, but the 
“if” does not quite have its English sense. 
{{lex|example-random-id-FXSC}} is true so long as John is a man, even if James is not a woman; likewise, it is true just because James is not a woman, regardless of John's gender. This kind of 
“if-then” is technically known as a 
“material conditional”.

Since James is not a woman (by our assertions in 
{{ls|section-connectives-introduction}}), the English sentence 
“John is a man if James is a woman” seems to be neither true nor false, since it assumes something which is not true. It turns out to be most convenient to treat this 
“if” as TTFT, which on investigation means that 
{{lex|example-random-id-FXSC}} is true. 
{{lex|example-random-id-EdY5}}, however, is equally true:

{{dsp|example-random-id-EdY5}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-EdY5}}
{{judri|c14e4d9}}
:'''la djan. ninmu .ijanai la djeimyz. ninmu'''
:''John is a woman if James is a woman.''

{{ind|general-imported|false statement|implications of}}  {{ind|general-imported|principle of consistency|of logical-if statements}} This can be thought of as a principle of consistency, and may be paraphrased as follows: 

“If a false statement is true, any statement follows from it.” All uses of English “if” must be considered very carefully when translating into Lojban to see if they really fit this Lojban mold.

{{ind|general-imported|only if|compared with if … then}}  {{ind|general-imported|if … then|compared with only if}} 
{{lex|example-random-id-9CCS}}, which uses the TFTT truth function, is subject to the same rules: the stated gloss of TFTT as 
“only if” works naturally only when the right-hand bridi is false; if it is true, the left-hand bridi may be either true or false. The last gloss of 
{{lex|example-random-id-9CCS}} illustrates the use of 
“if ... then” as a more natural substitute for “only if”.

{{dsp|example-random-id-9CCS}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-9CCS}}
{{judri|c14e4d10}}
:'''la djan. nanmu .inaja la djeimyz. ninmu'''
:<code>John is-not-a-man or James is-a-woman.</code>
:''John is a man only if James is a woman.''
:''If John is a man, then James is a woman.''

{{ind|general-imported|se|in logical connective to exchange sentences}} The following example illustrates the use of 
{{vla|se}} to, in effect, exchange the two sentences. The normal use of 
{{vla|se}} is to (in effect) transpose places of a bridi, as explained in 
{{ls|section-place-conversion}}.

{{dsp|example-random-id-z43X}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-z43X}}
{{judri|c14e4d11}}
:'''la djan. nanmu .iseju la djeimyz. ninmu'''
:''Whether or not John is a man, James is a woman.''

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|nai}}  {{ind|general-imported|na|order in logical connectives with se}}  {{ind|general-imported|se|order in logical connectives with na}} If both 
{{vla|na}} and 
{{vla|se}} are present, which is legal but never necessary, 
{{vla|na}} would come before 
{{vla|se}}.

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|JA selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|I selma'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|ijeks|syntax of}} The full syntax of ijeks, therefore, is:

{{grammar|.i [na] [se] JA [nai]}}
where the cmavo in brackets are optional.

{{ssp|section-forethought-bridi-connection}}
==Forethought bridi connection==

{{ind|general-imported|forethought connectives|contrasted with afterthought connectives}}  {{ind|general-imported|afterthought connectives|contrasted with forethought connectives}} Many concepts in Lojban are expressible in two different ways, generally referred to as 
“afterthought” and 
“forethought”. 
{{ls|section-bridi-connection}} discussed what is called 
“afterthought bridi logical connection”. The word 

“afterthought” is used because the connective cmavo and the second bridi were added, as it were, afterwards and without changing the form of the first bridi. This form might be used by someone who makes a statement and then wishes to add or qualify that statement after it has been completed. Thus,

{{dsp|example-random-id-dp8V}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-dp8V}}
{{judri|c14e5d1}}
:'''la djan. nanmu'''

is a complete bridi, and adding an afterthought connection to make

{{dsp|example-random-id-7h3s}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-7h3s}}
{{judri|c14e5d2}}
:'''la djan. nanmu .ija la djeimyz. ninmu'''
:''John is a man or James is a woman (or both)''

provides additional information without requiring any change in the form of what has come before; changes which may not be possible or practical, especially in speaking. (The meaning, however, may be changed by the use of a negating connective.) Afterthought connectives make it possible to construct all the important truth-functional relationships in a variety of ways.

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|JA selma'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|afterthought bridi connectives|contrasted with forethought bridi connectives}}  {{ind|general-imported|forethought bridi connectives|contrasted with afterthought bridi connectives}}  {{ind|general-imported|gek bridi connectives|contrasted with ijeks}}  {{ind|general-imported|ijek bridi connectives|contrasted with geks}}  {{ind|general-imported|gek|definition}} In forethought style the speaker decides in advance, before expressing the first bridi, that a logical connection will be expressed. Forethought and afterthought connectives are expressed with separate selma'o. The forethought logical connectives corresponding to afterthought ijeks are geks:

{{dsp|example-random-id-mYeS}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-mYeS}}
{{judri|c14e5d3}}
:'''ga la djan. nanmu gi la djeimyz. ninmu'''
:''Either John is a man or James is a woman (or both).''

{{vla|ga}} is the cmavo which represents the 
A truth function in selma'o GA. The word 
{{vla|gi}} does not belong to GA at all, but constitutes its own selma'o: it serves only to separate the two bridi without having any content of its own. The English translation of 
{{vla|ga}}&hellip;{{vla|gi}} is 
“either ... or”, but in the English form the truth function is specified both by the word 
“either” and by the word 
“or”: not so in Lojban.

{{ind|general-imported|i|regarding forethought bridi connection}}  {{ind|general-imported|forethought bridi connection|as grammatically one sentence}} Even though two bridi are being connected, geks and giks do not have any 

{{vla|i}} in them. The forethought construct binds up the two bridi into a single sentence as far as the grammar is concerned.

Some more examples of forethought bridi connection are:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qGLh}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qGLh}}
{{judri|c14e5d4}}
:'''ge la djan. nanmu gi la djeimyz. ninmu'''
:''(It is true that) both John is a man and James is a woman.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qgMN}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qgMN}}
{{judri|c14e5d5}}
:'''gu la djan. nanmu gi la djeimyz. ninmu'''
:''It is true that John is a man, whether or not James is a woman.''

It is worth emphasizing that 
{{lex|example-random-id-qgMN}} does not assert that James is (or is not) a woman. The 
{{vla|gu}} which indicates that 
:{{jbo|la djeimyz. ninmu}} may be true or false is unfortunately rather remote from the bridi thus affected.

Perhaps the most important of the truth functions commonly expressed in forethought is TFTT, which can be paraphrased as 
“if ... then ...”:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Xcg1}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Xcg1}}
{{judri|c14e5d6}}
:'''ganai la djan. nanmu gi la djeimyz. ninmu'''
:<code>Either John is not a man, or James is a woman.</code>
:''If John is a man, then James is a woman.''

{{ind|general-imported|nai|placement in afterthought bridi connection contrasted with forethought}}  {{ind|general-imported|nai|placement in forethought bridi connection contrasted with afterthought}} Note the placement of the 
{{vla|nai}} in 
{{lex|example-random-id-Xcg1}}. When added to afterthought selma'o such as JA, a following 
{{vla|nai}} negates the second bridi, to which it is adjacent. Since GA cmavo precede the first bridi, a following 
{{vla|nai}} negates the first bridi instead.

{{ind|general-imported|logical connectives|negated first sentence as a potential problem for understanding}} Why does English insist on forethought in the translation of 
{{lex|example-random-id-Xcg1}}? Possibly because it would be confusing to seemingly assert a sentence and then make it conditional (which, as the Lojban form shows, involves a negation). Truth functions which involve negating the first sentence may be confusing, even to the Lojbanic understanding, when expressed using afterthought.

{{ind|general-imported|if … then|logical connectives contrasted with other translations}} It must be reiterated here that not every use of English 
“if ... then” is properly translated by 

{{vla|.i}}{{vla|na}}{{vla|ja}} or 
{{vla|ganai}}&hellip;{{vla|gi}}; anything with implications of time needs a somewhat different Lojban translation, which will be discussed in 
{{ls|section-sumtcita}}. Causal sentences like 
“If you feed the pig, then it will grow” are not logical connectives of any type, but rather need a translation using 

{{vla|rinka}} as the selbri joining two event abstractions, thus:

{{dsp|example-random-id-TQP9}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-TQP9}}
{{judri|c14e5d7}}
:'''le nu do cidja dunda fi le xarju cu rinka le nu ri ba banro'''
:<code>The event-of (you food-give to the pig) causes the event-of (it will grow).</code>

Causality is discussed in far more detail in 
{{ls|section-causals}}.

{{lex|example-random-id-I2jU}} and 
{{lex|example-random-id-Tiz6}} illustrates a truth function, FTTF, which needs to negate either the first or the second bridi. We already understand how to negate the first bridi:

{{dsp|example-random-id-I2jU}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-I2jU}}
{{judri|c14e5d8}}
:'''gonai la djan. nanmu gi la djeimyz. ninmu'''
:<code>John is-not-a-man if-and-only-if James is-a-woman.</code>
:''Either John is a man or James is a woman but not both.''

How can the second bridi be negated? By adding 
:{{jbo|-nai}} to the 
{{vla|gi}}.

{{dsp|example-random-id-Tiz6}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Tiz6}}
{{judri|c14e5d9}}
:'''go la djan. nanmu ginai la djeimyz. ninmu'''
:<code>John is-a-man if-and-only-if James is-not-a-woman.</code>
:''Either John is a man or James is a woman but not both.''

{{ind|general-imported|gik|definition}} A compound cmavo based on 
{{vla|gi}} is called a gik; the only giks are 

{{vla|gi}} itself and 
{{vla|gi}}{{vla|nai}}.

Further examples:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qgmv}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qgmv}}
{{judri|c14e5d10}}
:'''ge la djan. nanmu ginai la djeimyz. ninmu'''
:<code>John is-a-man and James is-not-a-woman.</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qgMy}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qgMy}}
{{judri|c14e5d11}}
:'''ganai la djan. nanmu ginai la djeimyz. ninmu'''
:<code>John is-not-a-man or James is-not-a-woman.</code>

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|GA selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|nai}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|se}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|GA selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|ganai}}  {{ind|general-imported|geks|syntax of}} The syntax of geks is:

{{grammar|[se] GA [nai]}}
{{ind|lojban-word-imported|nai}}  {{ind|general-imported|giks|syntax of}} and of giks (which are not themselves connectives, but part of the machinery of forethought connection) is:

{{grammar|{{vla|gi}} [nai]}}

{{ssp|section-sumti-connection}}
==sumti connection==

{{ind|general-imported|bridi logical connection|compared with sumti logical connections}}  {{ind|general-imported|sumti logical connection|compared with bridi logical connections}}  {{ind|general-imported|sumti logical connection|rationale for}}  {{ind|general-imported|sumti logical connection}} Geks and ijeks are sufficient to state every possible logical connection between two bridi. However, it is often the case that two bridi to be logically connected have one or more portions in common:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Ecnq}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Ecnq}}
{{judri|c14e6d1}}
:'''la djan. klama le zarci .ije la .alis. klama le zarci'''
:''John goes to the market, and Alice goes to the market.''

Here only a single sumti differs between the two bridi. Lojban does not require that both bridi be expressed in full. Instead, a single bridi can be given which contains both of the different sumti and uses a logical connective from a different selma'o to combine the two sumti:

{{dsp|example-random-id-JTIm}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-JTIm}}
{{judri|c14e6d2}}
:'''la djan .e la .alis. klama le zarci'''
:<code>John and Alice go-to the market.</code>

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|A selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|.e}}  {{ind|general-imported|logical connection|transformation between forms}} 
{{lex|example-random-id-JTIm}} means exactly the same thing as 
{{lex|example-random-id-Ecnq}}: one may be rigorously transformed into the other without any change of logical meaning. This rule is true in general for every different kind of logical connection in Lojban; all of them, with one exception (See {{ls|section-tanru}}), can always be transformed into a logical connection between sentences that expresses the same truth function.

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|A selma'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|eks|in sumti forethought logical connection}}  {{ind|general-imported|sumti connection|afterthought}} The afterthought logical connectives between sumti are eks, which contain a connective cmavo of selma'o A. If ijeks were used in 
{{lex|example-random-id-JTIm}}, the meaning would be changed:

{{dsp|example-random-id-7KHA}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-7KHA}}
{{judri|c14e6d3}}
:'''la djan. .ije la .alis. klama le zarci'''
:<code>John [is/does something]. And Alices goes-to the market.</code>

leaving the reader uncertain why John is mentioned at all.

Any ek may be used between sumti, even if there is no direct English equivalent:

{{dsp|example-random-id-BDLS}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-BDLS}}
{{judri|c14e6d4}}
:'''la djan. .o la .alis. klama le zarci'''
:<code>John if-and-only-if Alice goes-to the market.</code>
:''John goes to the market if, and only if, Alice does.''

The second line of 
{{lex|example-random-id-7KHA}} is highly stilted English, but the first line (of which it is a literal translation) is excellent Lojban.

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|GA selma'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|geks|in forethought sumti connection}}  {{ind|general-imported|sumti connection|forethought}} What about forethought sumti connection? As is the case for bridi connection, geks are appropriate. They are not the only selma'o of forethought logical-connectives, but are the most commonly used ones.

{{dsp|example-random-id-YEa4}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-YEa4}}
{{judri|c14e6d5}}
:'''ga la djan. gi la .alis. klama le zarci'''
:<code>Either John or Alice (or both) goes-to the market.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|se writing convention|in eks}}  {{ind|general-imported|na writing convention|in eks}} Of course, eks include all the same patterns of compound cmavo that ijeks do. When 
{{vla|na}} or 
{{vla|se}} is part of an ek, a special writing convention is invoked, as in the following example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-caoY}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-caoY}}
{{judri|c14e6d6}}
:'''la djan. na.a la .alis. klama le zarci'''
:<code>John only if Alice goes-to the market.</code>
:''John goes to the market only if Alice does.''

Note the period in 
{{vla|na}}{{vla|.a}}. The cmavo of A begin with vowels, and therefore must always be preceded by a pause. It is conventional to write all connective compounds as single words (with no spaces), but this pause must still be marked in writing as in speech; otherwise, the 
{{vla|na}} and 
{{vla|a}} would tend to run together.

{{ssp|section-more-propositions}}
==More than two propositions==
{{ind|general-imported|logical connectives|more than 2 sentences}} So far we have seen logical connectives used to connect exactly two sentences. How about connecting three or more? Is this possible in Lojban? The answer is yes, subject to some warnings and some restrictions.

{{ind|general-imported|logical connectives|associative}} Of the four primitive truth functions A, E, O, and U, all but O have the same truth values no matter how their component sentences are associated in pairs. Therefore,

{{dsp|example-random-id-9tHr}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-9tHr}}
{{judri|c14e7d1}}
:'''mi dotco .ije mi ricfu .ije mi nanmu'''
:<code>I am-German. And I am-rich. And I am-a-man.</code>

means that all three component sentences are true. Likewise,

{{dsp|example-random-id-MCsf}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-MCsf}}
{{judri|c14e7d2}}
:'''mi dotco .ija mi ricfu .ija mi nanmu'''
:<code>I am-German. Or I am-rich. Or I am-a-man.</code>

means that one or more of the component sentences is true.

{{ind|general-imported|logical connectives|equivalence relation on 3 sentences}}  {{ind|general-imported|logical connectives|non-associative}} 
O, however, is different. Working out the truth table for

{{dsp|example-random-id-3zE1}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-3zE1}}
{{judri|c14e7d3}}
:'''mi dotco .ijo mi ricfu .ijo mi nanmu'''
:<code>I am-German. If-and-only-if I am-rich. If-and-only-if I am-a-man.</code>

shows that 
{{lex|example-random-id-3zE1}} does not mean that either I am all three of these things or none of them; instead, an accurate translation would be:

:''Of the three properties &ndash; German-ness, wealth, and manhood &ndash; I possess either exactly one or else all three.''
{{ind|general-imported|logical connection|negation in connecting more than 2 sentences}}  {{ind|general-imported|logical connection|of more than 2 sentences|things to avoid}} Because of the counterintuitiveness of this outcome, it is safest to avoid 
O with more than two sentences. Likewise, the connectives which involve negation also have unexpected truth values when used with more than two sentences.

{{ind|general-imported|logical connection|of more than 2 sentences|all or none}} In fact, no combination of logical connectives can produce the 
“all or none” interpretation intended (but not achieved) by 
{{lex|example-random-id-3zE1}} without repeating one of the bridi. See {{lex|example-random-id-KyHw}}.

There is an additional difficulty with the use of more than two sentences. What is the meaning of:

{{ind|general-imported|logical connection of more than 2 sentences|mixed &quot;and&quot; and &quot;or&quot;}}

{{dsp|example-random-id-mLo1}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-mLo1}}
{{judri|c14e7d4}}
:'''mi nelci la djan. .ije mi nelci la martas. .ija mi nelci la meris.'''
:''I like John. And I like Martha. Or I like Mary.''

Does this mean:

{{dsp|example-random-id-BSuT}}
{{judri|c14e7d5}}
I like John, and I like either Martha or Mary or both.

Or is the correct translation:

{{dsp|example-random-id-dPcI}}
{{judri|c14e7d6}}
Either I like John and I like Martha, or I like Mary, or both.

{{ind|general-imported|logical connection|of more than 2 sentences|forethought}}  {{ind|general-imported|logical connectives|pairing from left}} 
{{lex|example-random-id-dPcI}} is the correct translation of 
{{lex|example-random-id-mLo1}}. The reason is that Lojban logical connectives pair off from the left, like many constructs in the language. This rule, called the left-grouping rule, is easy to forget, especially when intuition pulls the other way. Forethought connectives are not subject to this problem:

{{dsp|example-random-id-487z}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-487z}}
{{judri|c14e7d7}}
:'''ga ge mi nelci la djan. gi mi nelci la martas. gi mi nelci la meris.'''
:''Either (Both I like John and I like Martha) or I like Mary.''

is equivalent in meaning to 
{{lex|example-random-id-mLo1}}, whereas

{{dsp|example-random-id-1Dd2}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-1Dd2}}
{{judri|c14e7d8}}
:'''ge mi nelci la djan. gi ga mi nelci la martas. gi mi nelci la meris.'''
:''Both I like John and (Either I like Martha or I like Mary).''

is not equivalent to 
{{lex|example-random-id-mLo1}}, but is instead a valid translation into Lojban, using forethought, of 
{{lex|example-random-id-BSuT}}.

{{ssp|section-afterthought-connectives-grouping}}
==Grouping of afterthought connectives==
{{ind|general-imported|bo|in logical connectives}}  {{ind|general-imported|logical connection|with bo|precedence}}  {{ind|general-imported|logical connectives|grouping with bo}} There are several ways in Lojban to render 
{{lex|example-random-id-BSuT}} using afterthought only. The simplest method is to make use of the cmavo 
{{vla|bo}} (of selma'o BO). This cmavo has several functions in Lojban, but is always associated with high precedence and short scope. In particular, if 
{{vla|bo}} is placed after an ijek, the result is a grammatically distinct kind of ijek which overrides the regular left-grouping rule. Connections marked with 
{{vla|bo}} are interpreted before connections not so marked. 
{{lex|example-random-id-Uu7D}} is equivalent in meaning to 
{{lex|example-random-id-1Dd2}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Uu7D}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Uu7D}}
{{judri|c14e8d1}}
:'''mi nelci la djan. .ije mi nelci la martas. .ijabo mi nelci la meris.'''
:''I like John, and I like Martha or I like Mary.''

The English translation feebly indicates with a comma what the Lojban marks far more clearly: the 
“I like Martha” and 
“I like Mary” sentences are joined by 
{{vla|.i}}{{vla|ja}} first, before the result is joined to 
“I like John” by 
{{vla|.i}}{{vla|je}}.

Eks can have 
{{vla|bo}} attached in exactly the same way, so that 
{{lex|example-random-id-JVhK}} is equivalent in meaning to {{lex|example-random-id-Uu7D}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-JVhK}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-JVhK}}
{{judri|c14e8d2}}
:'''mi nelci la djan. .e la martas. .abo la meris.'''

{{ind|general-imported|bo and forethought connectives}}  {{ind|general-imported|forethought connectives and bo}} Forethought connectives, however, never can be suffixed with 
{{vla|bo}}, for every use of forethought connectives clearly indicates the intended pattern of grouping.

What happens if 
{{vla|bo}} is used on both connectives, giving them the same high precedence, as in 
{{lex|example-random-id-YJeE}}?

{{dsp|example-random-id-YJeE}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-YJeE}}
{{judri|c14e8d3}}
:'''mi nelci la djan. .ebo la martas. .abo la meris.'''

{{ind|general-imported|logical connectives|right-grouping with bo}}  {{ind|general-imported|bo|right-grouping}} Does this wind up meaning the same as 
{{lex|example-random-id-mLo1}} and 
{{lex|example-random-id-dPcI}}? Not at all. A second rule relating to 
{{vla|bo}} is that where several 
{{vla|bo}}-marked connectives are used in succession, the normal Lojban left-grouping rule is replaced by a right-grouping rule. As a result, 

{{lex|example-random-id-YJeE}} in fact means the same as 
{{lex|example-random-id-Uu7D}} and 
{{lex|example-random-id-JVhK}}. This rule may be occasionally exploited for special effects, but is tricky to keep straight; in writing intended to be easy to understand, multiple consecutive connectives marked with 
{{vla|bo}} should be avoided.

{{ind|general-imported|complex logical connectives|grouping with parentheses}}  {{ind|general-imported|logical connection|grouping strategies for complex cases contrasted}}  {{ind|general-imported|complex logical connection|grouping strategies contrasted}} The use of 
{{vla|bo}}, therefore, gets tricky in complex connections of more than three sentences. Looking back at the English translations of 
{{lex|example-random-id-487z}} and 
{{lex|example-random-id-1Dd2}}, parentheses were used to clarify the grouping. These parentheses have their Lojban equivalents, two sets of them actually. 
{{vla|tu'e}} and 
{{vla|tu'u}} are used with ijeks, and 
{{vla|ke}} and 
{{vla|ke'e}} with eks and other connectives to be discussed later. ( 
{{vla|ke}} and 
{{vla|ke'e}} are also used in other roles in the language, but always as grouping markers). Consider the English sentence:

{{dsp|example-random-id-aqIg}}
{{judri|c14e8d4}}
I kiss you and you kiss me, if I love you and you love me.

{{ind|general-imported|complex logical connectives|grouping with bo}} where the semantics tells us that the instances of 
“and” are meant to have higher precedence than that of 
“if”. If we wish to express 
{{lex|example-random-id-aqIg}} in afterthought, we can say:

{{dsp|example-random-id-1PSK}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-1PSK}}
{{judri|c14e8d5}}
:'''mi cinba do .ije[bo] do cinba mi .ijanai mi prami do .ijebo do prami mi'''
:''I kiss you and you kiss me, if I love you and you love me.''

marking two of the ijeks with 
{{vla|bo}} for high precedence. (The first 
{{vla|bo}} is not strictly necessary, because of the left-grouping rule, and is shown here in brackets.)

{{ind|general-imported|complex logical connectives|grouping with parentheses}} But it may be clearer to use explicit parenthesis words and say:

{{dsp|example-random-id-erTb}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-erTb}}
{{judri|c14e8d6}}
:'''tu'e mi cinba do .ije do cinba mi tu'u .ijanai tu'e mi prami do .ije do prami mi [tu'u]'''
:<code>( I kiss you and you kiss me ) if ( I love you and you love me ).</code>

where the 
{{vla|tu'e}}&hellip;{{vla|tu'u}} pairs set off the structure. The cmavo 
{{vla|tu'u}} is an elidable terminator, and its second occurrence in 
{{lex|example-random-id-erTb}} is bracketed, because all terminators may be elided at the end of a text.

In addition, parentheses are a general solution: multiple parentheses may be nested inside one another, and additional afterthought material may be added without upsetting the existing structure. Neither of these two advantages apply to 
{{vla|bo}} grouping. In general, afterthought constructions trade generality for simplicity.

Because of the left-grouping rule, the first set of 
{{vla|tu'e}}&hellip;{{vla|tu'u}} parentheses may actually be left off altogether, producing:

{{dsp|example-random-id-QGBz}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-QGBz}}
{{judri|c14e8d7}}
:'''mi cinba do .ije do cinba mi .ijanai tu'e mi prami do .ije do prami mi [tu'u]'''
:<code>I kiss you and you kiss me if ( I love you and you love me ).</code>

What about parenthesized sumti connection? Consider

{{dsp|example-random-id-y9CC}}
{{judri|c14e8d8}}
I walk to either the market and the house, or the school and the office.

{{ind|general-imported|sumti|beginning with &quot;ke&quot;}}  {{ind|general-imported|logical connection|of sumti|restriction on ke}}  {{ind|general-imported|logical connection|of sumti|grouping with parentheses}} Two pairs of parentheses, analogous to 
{{lex|example-random-id-erTb}}, would seem to be the right approach. However, it is a rule of Lojban grammar that a sumti may not begin with 
{{vla|ke}}, so the first set of parentheses must be omitted, producing 
{{lex|example-random-id-0mJM}}, which is instead parallel to 
{{lex|example-random-id-QGBz}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-0mJM}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-0mJM}}
{{judri|c14e8d9}}
:'''mi dzukla le zarci .e le zdani .a ke le ckule .e le briju [ke'e]'''
:<code>I walk-to the market and the house or ( the school and the office ).</code>

{{ind|general-imported|ke in sumti grouping|where allowed}} If sumti were allowed to begin with 
{{vla|ke}}, unavoidable ambiguities would result, so 
{{vla|ke}} grouping of sumti is allowed only just after a logical connective. This rule does not apply to 
{{vla|tu'e}} grouping of bridi, as 
{{lex|example-random-id-erTb}} shows.

Now we have enough facilities to handle the problem of 
{{lex|example-random-id-3zE1}}: 
“I am German, rich, and a man &ndash; or else none of these.” The following paraphrase has the correct meaning:

{{dsp|example-random-id-KyHw}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-KyHw}}
{{judri|c14e8d10}}
{{ind|example|German rich man|example}}
:'''[tu'e] mi dotco .ijo mi ricfu [tu'u] .ije tu'e mi dotco .ijo mi nanmu [tu'u]'''
:<code>( I am-German if-and-only-if I am-rich ) and (I am-German if-and-only-if I am-a-man ).</code>

The truth table, when worked out, produces T if and only if all three component sentences are true or all three are false.

{{ssp|section-compound-bridi}}
==Compound bridi==
{{ind|general-imported|logical connection|of selbri}} So far we have seen how to handle two sentences that need have no similarity at all (bridi connection) and sentences that are identical except for a difference in one sumti (sumti connection). It would seem natural to ask how to logically connect sentences that are identical except for having different selbri.

{{ind|general-imported|compound bridi|definition}} Surprise! Lojban provides no logical connective that is designed to handle selbri and nothing else. Instead, selbri connection is provided as part of a more general-purpose mechanism called 
“compound bridi”. Compound bridi result from logically connecting sentences that differ in their selbri and possibly some of their sumti.

{{ind|general-imported|compound bridi|one sumti in common}} The simplest cases result when the x1 sumti is the only common point:

{{dsp|example-random-id-WebJ}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-WebJ}}
{{judri|c14e9d1}}
:'''mi klama le zarci .ije mi nelci la djan.'''
:''I go to the market, and I like John.''

is equivalent in meaning to the compound bridi:

{{dsp|example-random-id-9H9e}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-9H9e}}
{{judri|c14e9d2}}
:'''mi klama le zarci gi'e nelci la djan.'''
:<code>I go-to the market and like John.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|compound bridi|logical connection of}}  {{ind|general-imported|bridi-tail|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|gihek|definition}} As 
{{lex|example-random-id-9H9e}} indicates, giheks are used in afterthought to create compound bridi; 

{{vla|gi'e}} is the gihek corresponding to 
“and”. The actual phrases 
:{{jbo|klama le zarci}} and 
:{{jbo|nelci la djan.}} that the gihek connects are known as 
“bridi-tails”, because they represent (in this use) the 
“tail end” of a bridi, including the selbri and any following sumti, but excluding any sumti that precede the selbri:

{{dsp|example-random-id-F3RE}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-F3RE}}
{{judri|c14e9d3}}
:'''mi ricfu gi'e klama le zarci'''
:<code>I am-rich and go-to the market.</code>

In 
{{lex|example-random-id-F3RE}}, the first bridi-tail is 
{{vla|ricfu}}, a simple selbri, and the second bridi-tail is 
:{{jbo|klama le zarci}}, a selbri with one following sumti.

{{ind|general-imported|compound bridi|more than one sumti in common}} Suppose that more than a single sumti is identical between the two sentences:

{{dsp|example-random-id-PRxj}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-PRxj}}
{{judri|c14e9d4}}
:'''mi dunda le cukta do .ije mi lebna lo rupnu do'''
:<code>I give the book to-you, and I take some currency-units from-you.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|compound bridi with more than one sumti in common|with common sumti first}} In 
{{lex|example-random-id-PRxj}}, the first and last sumti of each bridi are identical; the selbri and the second sumti are different. By moving the final sumti to the beginning, a form analogous to 
{{lex|example-random-id-9H9e}} can be achieved:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Evo4}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Evo4}}
{{judri|c14e9d5}}
:'''fi do fa mi dunda le cukta gi'e lebna lo rupnu'''
:<code>to/from you I give the book and take some currency-units.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|tail-terms|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|logical connectives|bridi-tail connection}} where the 
{{vla|fi}} does not have an exact English translation because it merely places 
{{vla|do}} in the third place of both 
{{vla|lebna}} and 
{{vla|dunda}}. However, a form that preserves natural sumti order also exists in Lojban. Giheks connect two bridi-tails, but also allow sumti to be added following the bridi-tail. These sumti are known as tail-terms, and apply to both bridi. The straightforward gihek version of 
{{lex|example-random-id-PRxj}} therefore is:

{{dsp|example-random-id-DYBN}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-DYBN}}
{{judri|c14e9d6}}
:'''mi dunda le cukta gi'e lebna lo rupnu vau do'''
:<code>I (give the book) and (take some currency-units) to/from you.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|bridi-tails|eliding vau in}}  {{ind|general-imported|compound bridi with more than one sumti in common|with vau}} The 
{{vla|vau}} (of selma'o VAU) serves to separate the bridi-tail from the tail-terms. Every bridi-tail is terminated by an elidable 
{{vla|vau}}, but only in connection with compound bridi is it ever necessary to express this 

{{vla|vau}}. Thus:

{{dsp|example-random-id-L3eN}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-L3eN}}
{{judri|c14e9d7}}
:'''mi klama le zarci [vau]'''
:<code>I go-to the market.</code>

has a single elided 
{{vla|vau}}, and 
{{lex|example-random-id-9H9e}} is equivalent to:

{{dsp|example-random-id-RfIR}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-RfIR}}
{{judri|c14e9d8}}
:'''mi klama le zarci [vau] gi'e nelci la djan. [vau] [vau]'''

where the double 
{{vla|vau}} at the end of 
{{lex|example-random-id-RfIR}} terminates both the right-hand bridi-tail and the unexpressed tail-terms.

{{ind|general-imported|logical connectives|observative sentence connection}} A final use of giheks is to combine bridi-tails used as complete sentences, the Lojban observative:

{{dsp|example-random-id-rvUD}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-rvUD}}
{{judri|c14e9d9}}
:'''klama le zarci gi'e dzukla le briju'''
:<code>A goer to-the market and a walker to-the office.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|logical connection|of observatives|relation of first places}} Since x1 is omitted in both of the bridi underlying 
{{lex|example-random-id-rvUD}}, this compound bridi does not necessarily imply that the goer and the walker are the same. Only the presence of an explicit x1 (other than 

{{vla|zo'e}}, which is equivalent to omission) can force the goer and the walker to be identical.

{{ind|general-imported|relation of first places in logical connection of observatives|rationale}} A strong argument for this convention is provided by analysis of the following example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-cBrg}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-cBrg}}
{{judri|c14e9d10}}
:'''klama la nu,IORK. la finyks. gi'e klama la nu,IORK. la rom.'''
:<code>A goer to-New York from-Phoenix and a goer to-New York from-Rome.</code>

If the rule were that the x1 places of the two underlying bridi were considered identical, then (since there is nothing special about x1), the unspecified x4 (route) and x5 (means) places would also have to be the same, leading to the absurd result that the route from Phoenix to New York is the same as the route from Rome to New York. Inserting 
{{vla|da}}, meaning roughly 
“something”, into the x1 place cures the problem:

{{dsp|example-random-id-ij9G}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-ij9G}}
{{judri|c14e9d11}}
:'''da klama la nu,IORK. la finyks. gi'e klama la nu,IORK. la rom.'''
:<code>Something is-a-goer to-New York from-Phoenix and is-a-goer to-New York from-Rome.</code>

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|GIhA selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|nai}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|se}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|na}}  {{ind|general-imported|giheks|syntax of}} The syntax of giheks is:

{{grammar|[na] [se] GIhA [nai]}}
which is exactly parallel to the syntax of eks.

{{ssp|section-multiple-compound-bridi}}
==Multiple compound bridi==

{{ind|general-imported|compound bridi|multiple with bo}} Giheks can be combined with 
{{vla|bo}} in the same way as eks:

{{dsp|example-random-id-DpCN}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-DpCN}}
{{judri|c14e10d1}}
:'''mi nelci la djan. gi'e nelci la martas. gi'abo nelci la meris.'''
:''I like John and ( like Martha or like Mary ).''

{{ind|general-imported|compound bridi|multiple with ke…ke'e}} is equivalent in meaning to 
{{lex|example-random-id-Uu7D}} and 
{{lex|example-random-id-JVhK}}. Likewise, 
{{vla|ke}}&hellip;{{vla|ke'e}} grouping can be used after giheks:

{{dsp|example-random-id-rH4n}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-rH4n}}
{{judri|c14e10d2}}
:'''mi dzukla le zarci gi'e dzukla le zdani gi'a ke dzukla le ckule gi'e dzukla le briju [ke'e]'''
:<code>I walk-to the market and walk-to the house, or walk-to the school and walk-to the office.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|logical connection|of bridi-tails|restriction on ke}}  {{ind|general-imported|multiple compound bridi|restriction on ke}} is the gihek version of 
{{lex|example-random-id-0mJM}}. The same rule about using 
{{vla|ke}}&hellip;{{vla|ke'e}} bracketing only just after a connective applies to bridi-tails as to sumti, so the first two bridi-tails in 
{{lex|example-random-id-rH4n}} cannot be explicitly grouped; implicit left-grouping suffices to associate them.

{{ind|general-imported|compound bridi|separate tail-terms for bridi-tails}} Each of the pairs of bridi-tails joined by multiple giheks can have its own set of tail-terms:

{{dsp|example-random-id-1asY}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-1asY}}
{{judri|c14e10d3}}
{{ind|example|owe money|example}}
:'''mi dejni lo rupnu la djan. .inaja mi dunda le cukta la djan. .ijabo mi lebna le cukta la djan.'''
:<code>[If] I owe some currency-units to John, then I give the book to John or I take the book from John.</code>

is equivalent in meaning to:

{{dsp|example-random-id-901t}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-901t}}
{{judri|c14e10d4}}
:'''mi dejni lo rupnu nagi'a dunda gi'abo lebna vau le cukta vau la djan.'''
:<code>[If] I owe some currency-units then (give or take) a book to/from John.</code>

The literal English translation in 
{{lex|example-random-id-901t}} is almost unintelligible, but the Lojban is perfectly grammatical. 
{{vla|mi}} fills the x1 place of all three selbri; 
:{{jbo|lo rupnu}} is the x2 of 
{{vla|dejni}}, whereas 
:{{jbo|le cukta}} is a tail-term shared between 
{{vla|dunda}} and 
{{vla|lebna}}; 
:{{jbo|la djan.}} is a tail-term shared by 
{{vla|dejni}} and by 
:{{jbo|dunda gi'abo lebna}}. In this case, greater clarity is probably achieved by moving 
:{{jbo|la djan.}} to the beginning of the sentence, as in 
{{lex|example-random-id-Evo4}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-7NnV}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-7NnV}}
{{judri|c14e10d5}}
:'''fi la djan. fa mi dejni lo rupnu nagi'a dunda gi'abo lebna vau le cukta'''
:<code>To/from John, [if] I owe some currency-units then [I] give or take the book.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|logical connection|of bridi-tails|forethought}} Finally, what about forethought logical connection of bridi-tails? There is no direct mechanism for the purpose. Instead, Lojban grammar allows a pair of forethought-connected sentences to function as a single bridi-tail, and of course the sentences need not have terms before their selbri. For example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-4gJC}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-4gJC}}
{{judri|c14e10d6}}
:'''mi ge klama le zarci gi nelci la djan.'''
:''I both go to the market and like John.''

is equivalent in meaning to 
{{lex|example-random-id-9H9e}}.

Of course, either of the connected sentences may contain giheks:

{{dsp|example-random-id-mInd}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-mInd}}
{{judri|c14e10d7}}
:'''mi ge klama le zarci gi'e dzukla le zdani gi nelci la djan.'''
:''I both ( go to the market and walk to the house ) and like John.''

{{ind|general-imported|negating a forethought-connected bridi-tail pair}}  {{ind|general-imported|negating a forethought-connected sentence pair}} The entire gek-connected sentence pair may be negated as a whole by prefixing 
{{vla|na}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-DzgI}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-DzgI}}
{{judri|c14e10d8}}
:'''mi na ge klama le zarci gi dzukla le zdani'''
:<code>[False!] I both go to the market and walk to the house.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|compound bridi|separate tail-terms for forethought-connected bridi-tails}} Since a pair of sentences joined by geks is the equivalent of a bridi-tail, it may be followed by tail terms. The forethought equivalent of 
{{lex|example-random-id-DYBN}} is:

{{dsp|example-random-id-BUsi}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-BUsi}}
{{judri|c14e10d9}}
:'''mi ge dunda le cukta gi lebna lo rupnu vau do'''
:<code>I both ( give the book ) and ( take some currency-units ) to/from you.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|forethought connection|observatives}} Here is a pair of gek-connected observatives, a forethought equivalent of 

{{lex|example-random-id-rvUD}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-C5Wc}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-C5Wc}}
{{judri|c14e10d10}}
:'''ge klama le zarci gi dzukla le briju'''
:<code>Both a goer to-the market and a walker to-the office.</code>

Finally, here is an example of gek-connected sentences with both shared and unshared terms before their selbri:

{{dsp|example-random-id-eJyK}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-eJyK}}
{{judri|c14e10d11}}
:'''mi gonai le zarci cu klama gi le bisli cu dansu'''
:<code>I either-but-not-both to-the office go or on-the ice dance.</code>
:''I either go to the office or dance on the ice (but not both).''

{{ssp|section-termsets}}
==Termset logical connection==
So far we have seen sentences that differ in all components, and require bridi connection; sentences that differ in one sumti only, and permit sumti connection; and sentences that differ in the selbri and possibly one or more sumti, and permit bridi-tail connection. Termset logical connectives are employed for sentences that differ in more than one sumti but not in the selbri, such as:

{{dsp|example-random-id-G02C}}
{{judri|c14e11d1}}
I go to the market from the office and to the house from the school.

{{ind|general-imported|logical connection|termsets}}  {{ind|general-imported|termset|formation}}  {{ind|general-imported|term|definition}} The Lojban version of 
{{lex|example-random-id-G02C}} requires two termsets joined by a logical connective. A 
“term” is either a sumti or a sumti preceded by a tense or modal tag such as 
{{vla|pu}} or 
{{vla|bai}}. Afterthought termsets are formed by linking terms together by inserting the cmavo 
{{vla|ce'e}} (of selma'o CEhE) between each of them. Furthermore, the logical connective (which is a jek) must be prefixed by the cmavo 
{{vla|pe'e}} (of selma'o PEhE). (We could refer to the combination of 

{{vla|pe'e}} and a jek as a 

“pehejek”, I suppose.)

{{ind|general-imported|to the market from the office}}

{{dsp|example-random-id-UVPj}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-UVPj}}
{{judri|c14e11d2}}
:'''mi klama le zarci ce'e le briju pe'e je le zdani ce'e le ckule'''
:<code>I go to-the market [plus] from-the office [joint] and to-the house [plus] from-the school.</code>

The literal translation uses 
“[plus]” to indicate the termset connective, and 
“[joint]” to indicate the position of the logical connective joint. As usual, there is an equivalent bridi-connection form:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Bp2v}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Bp2v}}
{{judri|c14e11d3}}
:'''mi klama le zarci le briju .ije mi klama le zdani le ckule'''
:<code>I go to-the market from-the office, and I go to-the house from-the school.</code>

which illustrates that the two bridi differ in the x2 and x3 places only.

{{ind|general-imported|termset logical connection|unequal length}} What happens if the two joined sets of terms are of unequal length? Expanding to bridi connection will always make clear which term goes in which place of which bridi. It can happen that a sumti may fall in the x2 place of one bridi and the x3 place of another:

{{dsp|example-random-id-yYsr}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-yYsr}}
{{judri|c14e11d4}}
:'''mi pe'e ja do ce'e le zarci cu klama le briju'''
:<code>I [joint] or you to-the market [plus] go to/from-the office.</code>

can be clearly understood by expansion to:

{{dsp|example-random-id-NIuS}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-NIuS}}
{{judri|c14e11d5}}
:'''mi klama le briju .ija do le zarci cu klama le briju'''
:<code>I go to-the office, or you to-the market go from-the office.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|unequal termset connection|compared with compound bridi connection with unequal separate bridi-tails}} So 
:{{jbo|le briju}} is your origin but my destination, and thus falls in the x2 and x3 places of 
{{vla|klama}} simultaneously! This is legal because even though there is only one selbri, 
{{vla|klama}}, there are two distinct bridi expressed here. In addition, 
{{vla|mi}} in 
{{lex|example-random-id-yYsr}} is serving as a termset containing only one term. An analogous paradox applies to compound bridi with tail-terms and unequal numbers of sumti within the connected bridi-tails:

{{dsp|example-random-id-zsiy}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-zsiy}}
{{judri|c14e11d6}}
:'''mi klama le zarci gi'e dzukla vau le briju'''
:<code>I ( go to-the market and walk ) to/from-the office.</code>

means that I go to the market from the office, and I walk to the office; 

:{{jbo|le briju}} is the x3 place of 
{{vla|klama}} and the x2 place of 
{{vla|dzukla}}.

{{ind|general-imported|forethought termsets|logical connection of}}  {{ind|general-imported|logical connection|of forethought termsets}} Forethought termsets also exist, and use 
{{vla|nu'i}} of selma'o NUhI to signal the beginning and 
{{vla|nu'u}} of selma'o NUhU (an elidable terminator) to signal the end. Nothing is inserted between the individual terms: they simply sit side-by-side. To make a logical connection in a forethought termset, use a gek, with the gek just after the 
{{vla|nu'i}}, and an extra 
{{vla|nu'u}} just before the gik:

{{dsp|example-random-id-KeLv}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-KeLv}}
{{judri|c14e11d7}}
:'''mi klama nu'i ge le zarci le briju nu'u gi le zdani le ckule [nu'u]'''
:<code>I go [start termset] both to-the market from-the office [joint] and to-the house from-the school [end termset].</code>

Note that even though two termsets are being connected, only one 
{{vla|nu'i}} is used.

The grammatical uses of termsets that do not contain logical connectives are explained in 
{{ls|section-modal-connectives}},
{{ls|section-explicit-magnitudes}}, and
{{ls|section-quantifier-grouping}}.

{{ssp|section-tanru}}
==Logical connection within tanru==
{{ind|general-imported|logical connectives in tanru}} As noted at the beginning of 
{{ls|section-compound-bridi}}, there is no logical connective in Lojban that joins selbri and nothing but selbri. However, it is possible to have logical connectives within a selbri, forming a kind of tanru that involves a logical connection. Consider the simple tanru 
:{{jbo|blanu zdani}}, blue house. Now anything that is a blue ball, in the most ordinary understanding of the phrase at least, is both blue and a ball. And indeed, instead of 
:{{jbo|blanu bolci}}, Lojbanists can say 
:{{jbo|blanu je bolci}}, using a jek connective within the tanru. (We saw jeks used in 
{{ls|section-termsets}} also, but there they were always prefixed by 
{{vla|pe'e}}; in this section they are used alone.) Here is a pair of examples:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qGoH}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qGoH}}
{{judri|c14e12d1}}
{{ind|example|blue house|example}}
:'''ti blanu zdani'''
:<code>This is-a-blue type-of house.</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qgoW}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qgoW}}
{{judri|c14e12d2}}
{{ind|example|blue house|example}}
:'''ti blanu je zdani'''
:<code>This is-blue and a-house.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|unconnected tanru|contrasted with logically connected version}}  {{ind|general-imported|logical connection|in tanru|contrasted with unconnected version}} But of course 
{{lex|example-random-id-qGoH}} and 
{{lex|example-random-id-qgoW}} are not necessarily equivalent in meaning! It is the most elementary point about Lojban tanru that 
{{lex|example-random-id-qGoH}} might just as well mean

{{dsp|example-random-id-DxVB}}
{{judri|c14e12d3}}
This is a house for blue inhabitants.

and 
{{lex|example-random-id-qgoW}} certainly is not equivalent in meaning to 
{{lex|example-random-id-DxVB}}.

{{ind|general-imported|logical connection|in tanru|expandability of}} A full explanation of logical connection within tanru belongs rather to a discussion of selbri structure than to logical connectives in general. Why? Because although 
{{lex|example-random-id-qgoW}} happens to mean the same as

{{dsp|example-random-id-XXX6}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-XXX6}}
{{judri|c14e12d4}}
:'''ti blanu gi'e zdani'''

and therefore as

{{dsp|example-random-id-HqYS}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-HqYS}}
{{judri|c14e12d5}}
:'''ti blanu .ije ti zdani'''

the rule of expansion into separate bridi simply does not always work for tanru connection. Supposing Alice to be a person who lives in blue houses, then

{{dsp|example-random-id-DG5K}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-DG5K}}
{{judri|c14e12d6}}
:'''la .alis. cu blanu je zdani prenu'''
:<code>Alice is-a ( blue and house ) type-of-person.</code>

{{ind|general|tanru grouping|effect of jeks}}
would be true, because tanru grouping with a jek has higher precedence than unmarked tanru grouping, but:

{{dsp|example-random-id-eh2i}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-eh2i}}
{{judri|c14e12d7}}
:'''la .alis. cu blanu prenu .ije la .alis. cu zdani prenu'''
:<code>Alice is-a blue person, and Alice is-a house person.</code>

is probably false, because the blueness is associated with the house, not with Alice, even leaving aside the question of what it means to say 
“Alice is a blue person”. (Perhaps she belongs to the Blue team, or is wearing blue clothes.) The semantic ambiguity of tanru make such logical manipulations impossible.

{{ind|general-imported|logical connection|in tanru|grouping with bo}} It suffices to note here, then, a few purely grammatical points about tanru logical connection. 

{{vla|bo}} may be appended to jeks as to eks, with the same rules:

{{dsp|example-random-id-RNMY}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-RNMY}}
{{judri|c14e12d8}}
:'''la teris. cu ricfu je nakni jabo fetsi'''
:''Terry is rich and ( male or female ).''

{{ind|general-imported|logical connection|in tanru|grouping with ke}} 
The components of tanru may be grouped with 
{{vla|ke}} both before and after a logical connective:

{{dsp|example-random-id-JdID}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-JdID}}
{{judri|c14e12d9}}
:'''la .teris. cu [ke] ricfu ja pindi [ke'e] je ke nakni ja fetsi [ke'e]'''
:''Terry is (rich or poor) and (male or female).''

where the first 
{{vla|ke}}&hellip;{{vla|ke'e}} pair may be omitted altogether by the rule of left-grouping, but is optionally permitted. In any case, the last instance of 
{{vla|ke'e}} may be elided.

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|JA selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|nai}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|se}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|na}}  {{ind|general-imported|jeks|syntax of}} The syntax of jeks is:

{{grammar|[na] [se] JA [nai]}}
parallel to eks and giheks.

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|GUhA selma'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|guhek|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|forethought tanru connection}} Forethought tanru connection does not use geks, but uses guheks instead. Guheks have exactly the same form as geks:

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|GUhA selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|nai}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|se}}  {{ind|general-imported|guheks|syntax of}}
{{grammar|[se] GUhA [nai]}}
{{ind|general-imported|logical connection|of tanru as opposed to bridi-tail}}  {{ind|general-imported|logical connection|of bridi-tail as opposed to tanru}}  {{ind|general-imported|guheks for tanru connection|rationale}} Using guheks in tanru connection (rather than geks) resolves what would otherwise be an unacceptable ambiguity between bridi-tail and tanru connection:

{{dsp|example-random-id-mjog}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-mjog}}
{{judri|c14e12d10}}
:'''la .alis. gu'e ricfu gi fetsi'''
:''Alice is both rich and female.''

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|JA selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|GUhA selma'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|tanru connection grouping|guheks unmarked tanru}}  {{ind|general-imported|tanru grouping|guheks compared with jeks}} 
Note that giks are used with guheks in exactly the same way they are used with geks. Like jeks, guheks bind more closely than unmarked tanru grouping does:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Gyrc}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Gyrc}}
{{judri|c14e12d11}}
:'''la .alis. gu'e blanu gi zdani prenu'''
:<code>Alice is-a-(both blue and a-house) type-of-person.</code>

is the forethought version of 
{{lex|example-random-id-DG5K}}.

{{ind|general-imported|sumti logical connection|contrasted with tanru logical connection}}  {{ind|general-imported|tanru logical connection|contrasted with sumti logical connection}}  {{ind|general-imported|tanru|reducing logically connected sumti to|caveat}}  {{ind|general-imported|logical connection|of tanru|caveat}} A word of caution about the use of logically connected tanru within descriptions. English-based intuition can lead the speaker astray. In correctly reducing

{{dsp|example-random-id-8wbd}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-8wbd}}
{{judri|c14e12d12}}
:'''mi viska pa nanmu .ije mi viska pa ninmu'''
:''I see a man, and I see a woman.''

to

{{dsp|example-random-id-qf3n}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qf3n}}
{{judri|c14e12d13}}
:'''mi viska pa nanmu .e pa ninmu'''
:''I see a man and a woman.''

there is a great temptation to reduce further to:

{{dsp|example-random-id-ag8r}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-ag8r}}
{{judri|c14e12d14}}
{{ind|example|man-woman|example}}
:'''mi viska pa nanmu je ninmu'''
:''I see a man and woman.''

But 
{{lex|example-random-id-ag8r}} means that you see one thing which is both a man and a woman simultaneously! A 
:{{jbo|nanmu je ninmu}} is a manwoman, a presumably non-existent creature who is both a 
{{vla|nanmu}} and a 
{{vla|ninmu}}.

{{ssp|section-truth-and-connective-questions}}
==Truth questions and connective questions==

So far we have addressed only sentences which are statements. Lojban, like all human languages, needs also to deal with sentences which are questions. There are many ways of asking questions in Lojban, but some of these (like questions about quantity, tense, and emotion) are discussed in other chapters.

{{ind|general-imported|truth questions|simple}} The simplest kind of question is of the type 
“Is it true that ...” where some statement follows. This type is called a 
“truth question”, and can be represented in English by 
{{lex|example-random-id-bMjE}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-bMjE}}
{{judri|c14e13d1}}
Is it true that Fido is a dog?

Is Fido a dog?

Note the two formulations. English truth questions can always be formed by prefixing 
“Is is true that” to the beginning of a statement; there is also usually a more idiomatic way involving putting the verb before its subject. 
“Is Fido a dog?” is the truth question corresponding to 
“Fido is a dog”. In Lojban, the equivalent mechanism is to prefix the cmavo 
{{vla|xu}} (of selma'o UI) to the statement:

{{dsp|example-random-id-gKaM}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-gKaM}}
{{judri|c14e13d2}}
:'''xu la faidon. gerku'''
:<code>Is-it-true-that Fido is-a-dog?</code>

{{lex|example-random-id-bMjE}} and 
{{lex|example-random-id-gKaM}} are equivalent in meaning.

{{ind|general-imported|truth questions|answering &quot;no&quot;}}  {{ind|general-imported|truth questions|answering &quot;yes&quot;}}  {{ind|general-imported|truth questions|as yes-or-no questions}} A truth question can be answered 
“yes” or 
“no”, depending on the truth or falsity, respectively, of the underlying statement. The standard way of saying 
“yes” in Lojban is 
{{vla|go'i}} and of saying 
“no” is 
{{vla|na}}{{vla|go'i}}. (The reasons for this rule are explained in 

{{ls|section-ri-gohi-series}}.) In answer to 
{{lex|example-random-id-gKaM}}, the possible answers are:

{{dsp|example-random-id-XSmq}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-XSmq}}
{{judri|c14e13d3}}
:'''go'i'''
:''Fido is a dog.''

and

{{dsp|example-random-id-WI3P}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-WI3P}}
{{judri|c14e13d4}}
:'''nago'i'''
:''Fido is not a dog.''

{{ind|general-imported|truth questions|contrasted with connection questions}} Some English questions seemingly have the same form as the truth questions so far discussed. Consider

{{dsp|example-random-id-mftC}}
{{judri|c14e13d5}}
{{ind|example|dog or cat|example}}
Is Fido a dog or a cat?

Superficially, 
{{lex|example-random-id-mftC}} seems like a truth question with the underlying statement:

{{dsp|example-random-id-n6Ec}}
{{judri|c14e13d6}}
{{ind|example|dog or cat|example}}
Fido is a dog or a cat.

By translating 
{{lex|example-random-id-n6Ec}} into Lojban and prefixing 
{{vla|xu}} to signal a truth question, we get:

{{dsp|example-random-id-hz4S}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-hz4S}}
{{judri|c14e13d7}}
{{ind|example|dog or cat|example}}
:'''xu la faidon. gerku gi'onai mlatu'''
:<code>Is-it-true-that Fido is-a-dog or is-a-cat (but not both)?</code>

Given that Fido really is either a dog or a cat, the appropriate answer would be 
{{vla|go'i}}; if Fido were a fish, the appropriate answer would be 
{{vla|na}}{{vla|go'i}}.

But that is not what an English-speaker who utters 
{{lex|example-random-id-mftC}} is asking! The true significance of 
{{lex|example-random-id-mftC}} is that the speaker desires to know the truth value of either of the two underlying bridi (it is presupposed that only one is true).

{{ind|general-imported|questions|connection}} Lojban has an elegant mechanism for rendering this kind of question which is very unlike that used in English. Instead of asking about the truth value of the connected bridi, Lojban users ask about the truth function which connects them. This is done by using a special question cmavo: there is one of these for each of the logical connective selma'o, as shown by the following table:
<tab class=wikitable>
cmavo	selma'o	subclass	meaning
'''ge'i'''	GA	forethought connective question
'''gi'i'''	GIhA	bridi-tail connective question
'''gu'i'''	GUhA	tanru forethought connective question
'''je'i'''	JA	tanru connective question
'''ji'''	A	sumti connective question
</tab>

{{ind|general-imported|connective question cmavo|departure from regularity of}} (This list unfortunately departs from the pretty regularity of the other cmavo for logical connection. The two-syllable selma'o, GIhA and GUhA, make use of the cmavo ending in 
“-i” which is not used for a truth function, but 
{{vla|gi}} and 
{{vla|i}} were not available, and different cmavo had to be chosen. This table must simply be memorized, like most other non-connective cmavo assignments.)

{{ind|general-imported|connective questions|answering}} One correct translation of 
{{lex|example-random-id-mftC}} employs a question gihek:

{{dsp|example-random-id-G1Xs}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-G1Xs}}
{{judri|c14e13d8}}
:'''la .alis gerku gi'i mlatu'''
:<code>Alice is-a-dog [truth function?] is-a-cat?</code>

Here are some plausible answers:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qGPp}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qGPp}}
{{judri|c14e13d9}}
:'''nagi'e'''
:''Alice is not a dog and is a cat.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qGPq}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qGPq}}
{{judri|c14e13d10}}
:'''gi'enai'''
:''Alice is a dog and is not a cat.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qgrw}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qgrw}}
{{judri|c14e13d11}}
:'''nagi'enai'''
:''Alice is not a dog and is not a cat.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qGRz}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qGRz}}
{{judri|c14e13d12}}
:'''nagi'o'''
:'''gi'onai'''
:''Alice is a dog or is a cat but not both (I'm not saying which).''

{{lex|example-random-id-qGRz}} is correct but uncooperative.

{{ind|general-imported|afterthought connectives|as complete grammatical utterance}}  {{ind|general-imported|connectives|as complete grammatical utterance}} As usual, Lojban questions are answered by filling in the blank left by the question. Here the blank is a logical connective, and therefore it is grammatical in Lojban to utter a bare logical connective without anything for it to connect.

The answer 
{{vla|gi'e}}, meaning that Alice is a dog and is a cat, is impossible in the real world, but for:

{{dsp|example-random-id-xtIf}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-xtIf}}
{{judri|c14e13d13}}
{{ind|example|coffee or tea|example}}
:'''do djica tu'a loi ckafi ji loi tcati'''
:<code>You desire something-about a-mass-of coffee [truth function?] a-mass-of tea?</code>
:''Do you want coffee or tea?''

the answer 
{{vla|e}}, meaning that I want both, is perfectly plausible, if not necessarily polite.

{{ind|general-imported|afterthought connection|contrasted with forethought for grammatical utterances}}  {{ind|general-imported|forethought connection|contrasted with afterthought for grammatical utterances}}  {{ind|general-imported|forethought connectives|as ungrammatical utterance}}  {{ind|general-imported|connectives|as ungrammatical utterance}} The forethought questions 
{{vla|ge'i}} and 

{{vla|gu'i}} are used like the others, but ambiguity forbids the use of isolated forethought connectives as answers &ndash; they sound like the start of forethought-connected bridi. So although 

{{lex|example-random-id-286J}} is the forethought version of 
{{lex|example-random-id-xtIf}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-286J}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-286J}}
{{judri|c14e13d14}}
:'''do djica tu'a ge'i loi ckafi gi loi tcati'''
:<code>You desire something-about [truth function?] a-mass-of coffee [or] a-mass-of tea?</code>

the answer must be in afterthought form.

{{ind|general-imported|connective questions|compared with other languages}} There are natural languages, notably Chinese, which employ the Lojbanic form of connective question. The Chinese sentence

{{dsp|example-random-id-HyVv}}
{{judri|c14e13d15}}
:''ni<sup>3</sup> zou<sup>3</sup> hai<sup>2</sup>shi pao<sup>3</sup>''

means 
“Do you walk or run?”, and is exactly parallel to the Lojban:

{{dsp|example-random-id-3jIq}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-3jIq}}
