{{judri|c14e13d16}}
:'''do cadzu gi'i bajra'''
:<code>You walk [or?] run?</code>

{{ind|general-imported|connective question answers|contrasted with other languages}} However, Chinese does not use logical connectives in the reply to such a question, so the resemblance, though striking, is superficial.

{{ind|general-imported|imperatives|and truth}}  {{ind|general-imported|truth|in imperative sentences}}  {{ind|general-imported|bridi connection|use of imperatives in}}  {{ind|general-imported|bridi connection|use of truth questions in}} Truth questions may be used in bridi connection. This form of sentence is perfectly legitimate, and can be interpreted by using the convention that a truth question is true if the answer is “yes” and false if the answer is {{vla|no}}. Analogously, an imperative sentence (involving the special pro-sumti {{vla|ko}}, which means “you” but marks the sentence as a command) is true if the command is obeyed, and false otherwise. A request of Abraham Lincoln's may be translated thus:

{{dsp|example-random-id-BPv0}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-BPv0}}
{{judri|c14e13d17}}
{{ind|example|if coffee|bring tea|example}}  
{{ind|example|Abraham Lincoln|example}}
:'''ganai ti ckafi gi ko bevri loi tcati mi .ije ganai ti tcati gi ko bevri loi ckafi mi'''
:<code>If this is-coffee then [you!] bring a-mass-of tea to-me, and if this is-tea then [you!] bring a-mass-of coffee to-me.</code>
:''If this is coffee, bring me tea; but if this is tea, bring me coffee.''

{{ind|general-imported|and|compared with but}}  {{ind|general-imported|but|compared with and}} In logical terms, however, 
“but” is the same as 
“and”; the difference is that the sentence after a 
“but” is felt to be in tension or opposition to the sentence before it. Lojban represents this distinction by adding the discursive cmavo 
{{vla|ku'i}} (of selma'o UI), which is explained in 

{{ls|section-discursives}}, to the logical 
{{vla|.i}}{{vla|je}}.)

{{ssp|section-non-logical-connectives}}
==Non-logical connectives==
{{ind|general-imported|and|as non-logical connective}} Way back in 
{{ls|section-connectives-introduction}}, the point was made that not every use of English 
“and”, 
“if ... then”, and so on represents a Lojban logical connective. In particular, consider the “and” of:

{{dsp|example-random-id-x6JW}}
{{judri|c14e14d1}}
{{ind|example|carried piano|example}}
John and Alice carried the piano.

{{ind|general-imported|mass|joining elements into a}} Given the nature of pianos, this probably means that John carried one end and Alice the other. So it is not true that:

{{dsp|example-random-id-58yv}}
{{judri|c14e14d2}}
John carried the piano, and Alice carried the piano.

which would mean that each of them carried the piano by himself/herself. Lojban deals with this particular linguistic phenomenon as a 
“mass”. John and Alice are joined together into a mass, John-and-Alice, and it is this mass which carried the piano, not either of them separately. The cmavo 
{{vla|joi}} (of selma'o JOI) is used to join two or more components into a mass:

{{dsp|example-random-id-pC5x}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-pC5x}}
{{judri|c14e14d3}}
:'''la djan. joi la .alis. cu bevri le pipno'''
:<code>John massed-with Alice carry the piano.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|components contrasted with mass|in properties of}}  {{ind|general-imported|mass contrasted with components|in properties of}}  {{ind|general-imported|supervising|as a contribution to mass action}} 
{{lex|example-random-id-pC5x}} covers the case mentioned, where John and Alice divide the labor; it also could mean that John did all the hauling and Alice did the supervising. This possibility arises because the properties of a mass are the properties of its components, which can lead to apparent contradictions: if John is small and Alice is large, then John-and-Alice is both small and large. Masses are also discussed in 

{{ls|section-masses}}.

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|JA selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|A selma'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|non-logical connection|in tanru|distinguishing from connection of sumti}}  {{ind|general-imported|non-logical connection|of sumti|distinguishing from connection in tanru}}  {{ind|general-imported|joi grammar|contrasted with jeks}}  {{ind|general-imported|joi grammar|contrasted with eks}}  {{ind|general-imported|non-logical connection|and elidability of terminators}} Grammatically, 
{{vla|joi}} can appear between two sumti (like an ek) or between two tanru components (like a jek). This flexibility must be paid for in the form of occasional terminators that cannot be elided:

{{ind|general-imported|terminators|eliding ku in non-logical connections}}

{{dsp|example-random-id-NN93}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-NN93}}
{{judri|c14e14d4}}
:'''le nanmu ku joi le ninmu [ku] cu klama le zarci'''
:<code>The man massed-with the woman go-to the market.</code>

The cmavo 
{{vla|ku}} is the elidable terminator for 
{{vla|le}}, which can almost always be elided, but not in this case. If the first 
{{vla|ku}} were elided here, Lojban's parsing rules would see {{jbo|le nanmu joi}} and assume that another tanru component is to follow; since the second 
{{vla|le}} cannot be part of a tanru, a parsing error results. No such problem can occur with logical connectives, because an ek signals a following sumti and a jek a following tanru component unambiguously.

{{ind|general-imported|joik|definition}} Single or compound cmavo involving members of selma'o JOI are called joiks, by analogy with the names for logical connectives. It is not grammatical to use joiks to connect bridi-tails.

{{ind|general-imported|tanru connection|connotation of non-logical}} In tanru, 
{{vla|joi}} has the connotation 
“mixed with”, as in the following example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Xxp2}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Xxp2}}
{{judri|c14e14d5}}
{{ind|example|blue and red|example}}
{{ind|example|mixed with|example}}  
:'''ti blanu joi xunre bolci'''
:<code>This is-a-(blue mixed-with red) ball.</code>
:''This is a blue and red ball.''

Here the ball is neither wholly blue nor wholly red, but partly blue and partly red. Its blue/redness is a mass property. (Just how blue something has to be to count as 
“wholly blue” is an unsettled question, though. A 
:{{jbo|blanu zdani}} may be so even though not every part of it is blue.)

There are several other cmavo in selma'o JOI which can be used in the same grammatical constructions. Not all of them are well-defined as yet in all contexts. All have clear definitions as sumti connectives; those definitions are shown in the following table:

<tab class=wikitable header=true>
A {{vla|joi}} B	the mass with components A and B
A {{vla|ce}} B	the set with elements A and B
A {{vla|ce'o}} B	the sequence with elements A and B in order
A {{vla|se}}{{vla|ce'o}} B	the sequence with elements B and A in order
A {{vla|jo'u}} B	A and B considered jointly
A {{vla|fa'u}} B	A and B respectively
A {{vla|se}}{{vla|fa'u}} B	B and A respectively
A {{vla|jo'e}} B	the union of sets A and B
A {{vla|ku'a}} B	the intersection of sets A and B
A {{vla|pi'u}} B	the cross product of sets A and B
A {{vla|se}}{{vla|pi'u}} B	the cross product of sets B and A
</tab>
{{ind|general-imported|joiks|use of &quot;se&quot; in}}  {{ind|general-imported|se|as grammatical in JOI compounds}} The cmavo 
{{vla|se}} is grammatical before any JOI cmavo, but only useful with those that have inherent order. Here are some examples of joiks:

{{dsp|example-random-id-cwG8}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-cwG8}}
{{judri|c14e14d6}}
{{ind|example|choose from|example}}
:'''mi cuxna la .alis. la frank. ce la .alis. ce la djeimyz.'''
:<code>I choose Alice from Frank and-member Alice and-member James.</code>
:''I choose Alice from among Frank, Alice, and James.''

{{ind|general-imported|mass|contrasted with set in distribution of properties}}  {{ind|general-imported|set|contrasted with mass in distribution of properties}}  {{ind|general-imported|set|as specified by members}} The x3 place of 
{{vla|cuxna}} is a set from which the choice is being made. A set is an abstract object which is determined by specifying its members. Unlike those of a mass, the properties of a set are unrelated to its members' properties: the set of all rats is large (since many rats exist), but the rats themselves are small. This chapter does not attempt to explain set theory (the mathematical study of sets) in detail: explaining propositional logic is quite enough for one chapter!

{{ind|general-imported|set|by listing members with ce}} In 
{{lex|example-random-id-cwG8}} we specify that set by listing the members with 
{{vla|ce}} joining them.

{{dsp|example-random-id-Emw0}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Emw0}}
{{judri|c14e14d7}}
{{ind|example|list|example}}
:'''ti liste mi ce'o do ce'o la djan.'''
:<code>This is-a-list-of me and-sequence you and-sequence John.</code>
:''This is a list of you, me, and John.''

{{ind|general-imported|set|contrasted with ordered sequence}}  {{ind|general-imported|mass|contrasted with ordered sequence}}  {{ind|general-imported|ordered sequence|contrasted with mass}}  {{ind|general-imported|ordered sequence|contrasted with set}}  {{ind|general-imported|ordered sequence|by listing members}}  {{ind|general-imported|sequence|as an abstract list}}  {{ind|general-imported|list|as a physical object}}  {{ind|general-imported|sequence|contrasted with list}}  {{ind|general-imported|list|contrasted with sequence}} The x2 place of 
{{vla|liste}} is a sequence of the things which are mentioned in the list. (It is worth pointing out that 
:{{jbo|lo liste}} means a physical object such as a grocery list: a purely abstract list is 
:{{jbo|lo porsi}}, a sequence.) Here the three sumti connected by 
{{vla|ce'o}} are in a definite order, not just lumped together in a set or a mass.

{{ind|general-imported|jo'u|result of connection with}}  {{ind|general-imported|jo'u|contrasted with ce'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|jo'u|contrasted with ce}}  {{ind|general-imported|jo'u|contrasted with joi}}  {{ind|general-imported|individuals into set|by non-logical connection}}  {{ind|general-imported|individuals into mass|by non-logical connection}}  {{ind|general-imported|non-logical connection|of individuals into set}}  {{ind|general-imported|non-logical connection|of individuals into mass}} So 
{{vla|joi}}, 
{{vla|ce}}, and 
{{vla|ce'o}} are parallel, in that the sumti connected are taken to be individuals, and the result is something else: a mass, a set, or a sequence respectively. The cmavo 

{{vla|jo'u}} serves as a fourth element in this pattern: the sumti connected are individuals, and the result is still individuals &ndash; but inseparably so. The normal Lojban way of saying that James and George are brothers is:

{{dsp|example-random-id-sy2V}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-sy2V}}
{{judri|c14e14d8}}
{{ind|example|brothers|example}}
:'''la djeimyz. bruna la djordj.'''
:<code>James is-the-brother-of George.</code>

possibly adding a discursive element meaning 
“and vice versa”. However, 
“James and George are brothers” cannot be correctly translated as:

{{dsp|example-random-id-1PHN}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-1PHN}}
{{judri|c14e14d9}}
{{ind|example|brothers|example}}
:'''la djeimyz. .e la djordj. bruna'''
:<code>James and George is-a-brother.</code>

since that expands to two bridi and means that James is a brother and so is George, but not necessarily of each other. If the 
{{vla|e}} is changed to 
{{vla|jo'u}}, however, the meaning of 

{{lex|example-random-id-sy2V}} is preserved:

{{dsp|example-random-id-gnwy}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-gnwy}}
{{judri|c14e14d10}}
{{ind|example|brothers|example}}
:'''la djeimyz. jo'u la djordj. cu remei bruna'''
:<code>James in-common-with George are-a-twosome type-of-brothers.</code>

The tanru 
:{{jbo|remei bruna}} is not strictly necessary in this sentence, but is used to make clear that we are not saying that James and George are both brothers of some third person not specified. Alternatively, we could turn the tanru around: the x1 place of 

{{vla|re}}{{vla|mei}} is a mass with two components, leading to:

{{dsp|example-random-id-t0FJ}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-t0FJ}}
{{judri|c14e14d11}}
{{ind|example|brothers|example}}
:'''la djeimyz. joi la djordj. cu bruna remei'''
:<code>James massed-with George are-a-brother type-of-twosome.</code>

where 
{{vla|joi}} is used to create the necessary mass.

{{ind|general-imported|respectively|specifying with fa'u}}  {{ind|general-imported|connection|non-distributed}} Likewise, 
{{vla|fa'u}} can be used to put two individuals together where order matters. Typically, there will be another 
{{vla|fa'u}} somewhere else in the same bridi:

{{dsp|example-random-id-MBsp}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-MBsp}}
{{judri|c14e14d12}}
{{ind|example|respectively|example}}
:'''la djeimyz. fa'u la djordj. prami la meris. fa'u la martas.'''
:<code>James jointly-in-order-with George loves Mary jointly-in-order-with Martha.</code>
:''James and George love Mary and Martha, respectively.''

{{ind|general-imported|.e|contrasted with fa'u}}  {{ind|general-imported|fa'u|contrasted with .e}} Here the information carried by the English adverb 
“respectively”, namely that James loves Mary and George loves Martha, is divided between the two occurrences of 
{{vla|fa'u}}. If both uses of 
{{vla|fa'u}} were to be changed to 
{{vla|e}}, we would get:

{{dsp|example-random-id-7bv3}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-7bv3}}
{{judri|c14e14d13}}
:'''la djeimyz. .e la djordj. prami la meris. .e la martas.'''
:''James and George love Mary and Martha.''

which can be transformed to four bridi:

{{dsp|example-random-id-I3gH}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-I3gH}}
{{judri|c14e14d14}}
:'''la djeimyz. prami la meris. .ije la djordj. prami la meris. .ije la djeimyz. prami la martas. .ije la djordj. prami la martas.'''
:''James loves Mary, and George loves Mary, and James loves Martha, and George loves Martha.''

which represents quite a different state of affairs from 
{{lex|example-random-id-MBsp}}. The meaning of 
{{lex|example-random-id-MBsp}} can also be conveyed by a termset:

{{dsp|example-random-id-nER7}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-nER7}}
{{judri|c14e14d15}}
:'''la djeimyz. ce'e la meris. pe'e .e la djordj. ce'e la martas. prami'''
:<code>James [plus] Mary [joint] and George [plus] Martha loves.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|termsets|compared to fa'u}}  {{ind|general-imported|fa'u|compared to termsets}} at the expense of re-ordering the list of names so as to make the pairs explicit. This option is not available when one of the lists is only described rather than enumerated:

{{dsp|example-random-id-1r61}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-1r61}}
{{judri|c14e14d16}}
:'''la djeimyz. fa'u la djordj. prami re mensi'''
:<code>James and-respectively George love two sisters.</code>

which conveys that James loves one sister and George the other, though we are not able to tell which of the sisters is which.

{{ssp|section-non-logical-continued}}
==More about non-logical connectives==
{{ind|general-imported|cross-product|of sets}}  {{ind|general-imported|intersection|of sets}}  {{ind|general-imported|union|of sets}}  {{ind|general-imported|set operations}} The final three JOI cmavo, 
{{vla|jo'e}}, {{vla|ku'a}}, and {{vla|pi'u}}, are probably only useful when talking explicitly about sets. They represent three standard set operators usually called “union”, “intersection”, and “cross product” (also known as “Cartesian product”). The union of two sets is a set containing all the members that are in either set; the intersection of two sets is a set containing all the members that are in both sets. The cross product of two sets is the set of all possible ordered pairs, where each ordered pair contains a single element from the first set followed by a single element from the second. This may seem very abstract; hopefully, the following examples will help:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qGSA}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qGSA}}
{{judri|c14e15d1}}
{{ind|example|rich and German|example}}
:'''lo'i ricfu ku jo'e lo'i dotco cu barda'''
:<code>The-set-of rich-things union the-set-of German-things is large.</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qgSe}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qgSe}}
{{judri|c14e15d2}}
{{ind|example|rich and German|example}}
:'''lo'i ricfu ku ku'a lo'i dotco cu cmalu'''
:<code>The set-of rich-things intersection the-set-of German-things is small.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|intersection of sets|compared with and}}  {{ind|general-imported|union of sets|compared with or}} There is a parallelism between logic and set theory that makes 
{{lex|example-random-id-qGSA}} and 
{{lex|example-random-id-qgSe}} equivalent respectively to:

{{dsp|example-random-id-azCQ}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-azCQ}}
{{judri|c14e15d3}}
:'''lo'i ricfu ja dotco cu barda'''
:<code>The-set-of rich-or-German-things is large.</code>

and

{{dsp|example-random-id-QjD7}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-QjD7}}
{{judri|c14e15d4}}
:'''lo'i ricfu je dotco cu cmalu'''
:<code>The-set-of rich-and-German-things is small.</code>

The following example uses 
:{{jbo|se remei}}, which is a set (not a mass) of two elements:

{{dsp|example-random-id-D9gz}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-D9gz}}
{{judri|c14e15d5}}
:'''la djeimyz. ce[bo] la djordj. pi'u la meris. cebo la martas. cu prami se remei'''
:<code>James and-set George cross-product Mary and-set Martha are-lover type-of-pairs.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|and|contrasted with cross-product}}  {{ind|general-imported|cross-product|contrasted with and}}  {{ind|general-imported|e|contrasted with pi'u}}  {{ind|general-imported|pi'u|contrasted with .e}} means that each of the pairs James/Mary, George/Mary, James/Martha, and George/Martha love each other. Therefore it is similar in meaning to 
{{lex|example-random-id-7bv3}}; however, that example speaks only of the men loving the women, not vice versa.

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|JOI selma'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|non-logical connectives|grouping}}  {{ind|general-imported|joiks|grouping}} Joiks may be combined with 
{{vla|bo}} or with 
{{vla|ke}} in the same way as eks and jeks; this allows grouping of non-logical connections between sumti and tanru units, in complete parallelism with logical connections:

{{dsp|example-random-id-mwpo}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-mwpo}}
{{judri|c14e15d6}}
:'''mi joibo do ce la djan. joibo la djein. cu gunma se remei'''
:<code>(I massed-with you) and (John massed-with Jane) are-a-mass type-of-two-set</code>

asserts that there is a set of two items each of which is a mass.

{{ind|general-imported|termsets|non-logical connection of}}  {{ind|general-imported|non-logical connection|of termsets}} Non-logical connection is permitted at the joint of a termset; this is useful for associating more than one sumti or tagged sumti with each side of the non-logical connection. The place structure of 

{{vla|casnu}} is:

<definition>{{vla|casnu}} :''the mass x1 discusses/talks about x2''
so the x1 place must be occupied by a mass (for reasons not explained here); however, different components of the mass may discuss in different languages. To associate each participant with his or her language, we can say:

{{dsp|example-random-id-sdba}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-sdba}}
{{judri|c14e15d7}}
{{ind|example|discuss in language|example}}
:'''mi ce'e bau la lojban. pe'e joi do ce'e bau la gliban. nu'u casnu'''
:<code>( I [plus] in-language Lojban massed-with you [plus] in-language English ) discuss.</code>

Like all non-logical connectives, the usage shown in 
{{lex|example-random-id-sdba}} cannot be mechanically converted into a non-logical connective placed at another location in the bridi. The forethought equivalent of 
{{lex|example-random-id-sdba}} is:

{{dsp|example-random-id-DgXI}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-DgXI}}
{{judri|c14e15d8}}
:'''nu'i joigi mi bau la lojban gi do bau la gliban. nu'u casnu'''

{{ind|general-imported|respectively|with different relationships}}  {{ind|general-imported|tagged sumti termsets|connecting with non-logical forethought connectives}}  {{ind|general-imported|non-logical forethought termsets|connecting tagged sumti}} Non-logical forethought termsets are also useful when the things to be non-logically connected are sumti preceded with tense or modal (BAI) tags:

{{dsp|example-random-id-wVSG}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-wVSG}}
{{judri|c14e15d9}}
:'''la djan. fa'u la frank. cusku nu'i bau la lojban. nu'u fa'u bai tu'a la djordj. [nu'u]'''
:<code>John respectively-with Frank express [start termset] in-language Lojban [joint] respectively-with under-compulsion-by George.</code>
:''John and Frank speak in Lojban and under George's compulsion, respectively.''

{{lex|example-random-id-wVSG}} associates speaking in Lojban with John, and speaking under George's compulsion with Frank. We do not know what language Frank uses, or whether John speaks under anyone's compulsion.

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|JOI selma'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|sequence of events|expressing non-time-related sequences}}  {{ind|general-imported|ice'o|contrasted with .ibabo}}  {{ind|general-imported|sentences|connecting non-logically}}  {{ind|general-imported|non-logical connectives|sentence}}  {{ind|general-imported|ijoik|definition}} Joiks may be prefixed with 
{{vla|i}} to produce ijoiks, which serve to non-logically connect sentences. The ijoik 

{{vla|.i}}{{vla|ce'o}} indicates that the event of the second bridi follows that of the first bridi in some way other than a time relationship (which is handled with a tense):

{{dsp|example-random-id-27xU}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-27xU}}
{{judri|c14e15d10}}
{{ind|example|list of things to do|example}}
{{ind|example|to-do list|example}}  
:'''mi ba gasnu la'edi'e .i tu'e kanji lo ni cteki .ice'o lumci le karce .ice'o dzukansa le gerku tu'u'''
:<code>I [future] do the-referent-of-the-following: ( Compute the quantity of taxes. And-then wash the car. And-then walkingly-accompany the dog. )</code>
:''List of things to do: Figure taxes. Wash car. Walk dog.''

{{ind|general-imported|tu'e|use in lists}}  {{ind|general-imported|tu'e|effect on di'e}}  {{ind|general-imported|di'e|effect of tu'e/tu'u on}}  {{ind|general-imported|lists|use of tu'e/tu'u in}} 
{{lex|example-random-id-27xU}} represents a list of things to be done in priority order. The order is important, hence the need for a sequence connective, but does not necessarily represent a time order (the dog may end up getting walked first). Note the use of 
{{vla|tu'e}} and 
{{vla|tu'u}} as general brackets around the whole list. This is related to, but distinct from, their use in 
{{ls|section-afterthought-connectives-grouping}}, because there is no logical connective between the introductory phrase 
:{{jbo|mi ba gasnu la'edi'e}} and the rest. The brackets effectively show how large an utterance the word 
{{vla|di'e}}, which means 

“the following utterance”, refers to.

Similarly, 
{{vla|.i}}{{vla|joi}} is used to connect sentences that represent the components of a joint event such as a joint cause: the Lojban equivalent of 
“Fran hit her head and fell out of the boat, so that she drowned” would join the events 
“Fran hit her head” and 
“Fran fell out of the boat” with 
{{vla|.i}}{{vla|joi}}.

{{ind|general-imported|scalar negation of non-logical connective}}  {{ind|general-imported|non-logical connectives|effect of nai on}}  {{ind|general-imported|joiks|effect of nai on}}  {{ind|general-imported|nai|effect on joiks}} The following 
{{vla|nai}}, if present, does not negate either of the things to be connected, but instead specifies that some other connection (logical or non-logical) is applicable: it is a scalar negation:

{{dsp|example-random-id-mMdb}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-mMdb}}
{{judri|c14e15d11}}
:'''mi jo'unai do cu remei'''
:<code>I in-common-with [not!] you are-a-twosome</code>

The result of 
:{{jbo|mi jo'u do}} would be two individuals, not a mass, therefore 

{{vla|jo'u}} is not applicable; 

{{vla|joi}} would be the correct connective.

{{ind|general-imported|connective answers|non-logical}}  {{ind|general-imported|connective questions|non-logical}} There is no joik question cmavo as such; however, joiks and ijoiks may be uttered in isolation in response to a logical connective question, as in the following exchange:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qGSm}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qGSm}}
{{judri|c14e15d12}}
:'''do djica tu'a loi ckafi ji loi tcati'''
:<code>You desire something-about a-mass-of coffee [what connective?] a-mass-of tea?</code>
:''Do you want coffee or tea?''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qgsp}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qgsp}}
{{judri|c14e15d13}}
{{ind|example|ugh|example}}
{{ind|example|coffee mixed with tea|example}} 
:'''joi'''
:<code>Mixed-mass-and.</code>
:''Both as a mass (i.e, mixed together).''

Ugh. (Or in Lojban: {{vla|.a'u}}{{vla|nai}}{{vla|sai}}{{vla|ro'o}}.)

{{ssp|section-non-logical-continued-continued}}
==Interval connectives and forethought non-logical connection==

{{ind|general-imported|intervals|expressed as endpoints}}  {{ind|general-imported|non-logical connectives|intervals}} In addition to the non-logical connectives of selma'o JOI explained in 
{{ls|section-non-logical-connectives}} and 
{{ls|section-non-logical-continued}}, there are three other connectives which can appear in joiks: 
{{vla|bi'i}}, 
{{vla|bi'o}}, and 
{{vla|mi'i}}, all of selma'o BIhI. The first two cmavo are used to specify intervals: abstract objects defined by two endpoints. The cmavo 

{{vla|bi'i}} is correct if the endpoints are independent of order, whereas 
{{vla|bi'o}} or 
{{vla|se}}{{vla|bi'o}} are used when order matters.

An example of 
{{vla|bi'i}} in sumti connection:

{{dsp|example-random-id-sHhA}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-sHhA}}
{{judri|c14e16d1}}
{{ind|example|between Dresden and Frankfurt|example}}
:'''mi ca sanli la drezdn. bi'i la frankfurt.'''
:<code>I [present] stand-on-surface Dresden [interval] Frankfurt.</code>
:''I am standing between Dresden and Frankfurt.''

{{ind|general-imported|non-logical connectives|un-ordered intervals}} In 
{{lex|example-random-id-sHhA}}, it is all the same whether I am standing between Dresden and Frankfurt or between Frankfurt and Dresden, so 

{{vla|bi'i}} is the appropriate interval connective. The sumti 
:{{jbo|la drezdn. bi'i la frankfurt.}} falls into the x2 place of 
{{vla|sanli}}, which is the surface I stand on; the interval specifies that surface by its limits. (Obviously, I am not standing on the whole of the interval; the x2 place of 
{{vla|sanli}} specifies a surface which is typically larger in extent than just the size of the stander's feet.)

{{dsp|example-random-id-rYv4}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-rYv4}}
{{judri|c14e16d2}}
{{ind|example|from one to two o'clock|example}}
:'''mi cadzu ca la pacac. bi'o la recac.'''
:<code>I walk simultaneous-with First-hour [ordered-interval] Second-hour.</code>
:''I walk from one o'clock to two o'clock.''

{{ind|general-imported|non-logical connectives|ordered intervals}} In 
{{lex|example-random-id-rYv4}}, on the other hand, it is essential that 
:{{jbo|la pacac.}} comes before 
:{{jbo|la recac.}}; otherwise we have an 11-hour (or 23-hour) interval rather than a one-hour interval. In this use of an interval, the whole interval is probably intended, or at least most of it.

{{lex|example-random-id-rYv4}} is equivalent to:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qqIr}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qqIr}}
{{judri|c14e16d3}}
:'''mi cadzu ca la recac. sebi'o la pacac.'''
:<code>I walk simultaneous-with Second-hour [reverse] [ordered] First-hour.</code>

English cannot readily express 
{{vla|se}}{{vla|bi'o}}, but its meaning can be understood by reversing the two sumti.

{{ind|general-imported|intervals|expressed as center and distance}} The third cmavo of selma'o BIhI, namely 
{{vla|mi'i}}, expresses an interval seen from a different viewpoint: not a pair of endpoints, but a center point and a distance. For example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-wm5E}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-wm5E}}
{{judri|c14e16d4}}
{{ind|example|bomb destroyed fifty miles|example}}
:'''le jbama pu daspo la .uacintyn. mi'i lo minli be li muno'''
:<code>The bomb [past] destroys Washington [center] what-is measured-in-miles by 50.</code>
:''The bomb destroyed Washington and fifty miles around.''

Here we have an interval whose center is Washington and whose distance, or radius, is fifty miles.

{{ind|general-imported|endpoints|inclusion in interval}}  {{ind|general-imported|interval|inclusion of endpoints}}  {{ind|general-imported|interval|open}}  {{ind|general-imported|interval|closed}}  {{ind|general-imported|open interval}}  {{ind|general-imported|closed interval}} In 
{{lex|example-random-id-sHhA}}, is it possible that I am standing in Dresden (or Frankfurt) itself? Yes. The connectives of selma'o BIhI are ambiguous about whether the endpoints themselves are included in or excluded from the interval. Two auxiliary cmavo 
{{vla|ga'o}} and 
{{vla|ke'i}} (of cmavo GAhO) are used to indicate the status of the endpoints: 
{{vla|ga'o}} means that the endpoint is included, 
{{vla|ke'i}} that it is excluded:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qGTc}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qGTc}}
{{judri|c14e16d5}}
:'''mi ca sanli la drezdn. ga'o bi'i ga'o la frankfurt.'''
:<code>I [present] stand Dresden [inclusive] [interval] [inclusive] Frankfurt.</code>
:''I am standing between Dresden and Frankfurt, inclusive of both.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qGtv}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qGtv}}
{{judri|c14e16d6}}
:'''mi ca sanli la drezdn. ga'o bi'i ke'i la frankfurt.'''
:<code>I [present] stand Dresden [inclusive] [interval] [exclusive] Frankfurt.</code>
:''I am standing between Dresden (inclusive) and Frankfurt (exclusive).''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qgUo}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qgUo}}
{{judri|c14e16d7}}
:'''mi ca sanli la drezdn. ke'i bi'i ga'o la frankfurt.'''
:<code>I [present] stand Dresden [exclusive] [interval] [inclusive] Frankfurt.</code>
:''I am standing between Dresden (exclusive) and Frankfurt (inclusive).''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qGvB}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qGvB}}
{{judri|c14e16d8}}
{{ind|example|between Dresden and Frankfurt|example}}
:'''mi ca sanli la drezdn. ke'i bi'i ke'i la frankfurt.'''
:<code>I [present] stand Dresden [exclusive] [interval] [exclusive] Frankfurt.</code>
:''I am standing between Dresden and Frankfurt, exclusive of both.''

{{ind|general-imported|GAhO selma'o|grammar of}} As these examples should make clear, the GAhO cmavo that applies to a given endpoint is the one that stands physically adjacent to it: the left-hand endpoint is referred to by the first GAhO, and the right-hand endpoint by the second GAhO. It is ungrammatical to have just one GAhO.

{{ind|general-imported|ke'i|etymology of}}  {{ind|general-imported|ga'o|etymology of}} (Etymologically, 
{{vla|ga'o}} is derived from 
{{vla|ganlo}}, which means 
“closed”, and 
{{vla|ke'i}} from 
{{vla|kalri}}, which means 
“open”. In mathematics, inclusive intervals are referred to as closed intervals, and exclusive intervals as open ones.)

{{ind|general-imported|BIhI selma'o|grammar of}} BIhI joiks are grammatical anywhere that other joiks are, including in tanru connection and (as ijoiks) between sentences. No meanings have been found for these uses.

{{ind|general-imported|intervals|effect of nai on}}  {{ind|general-imported|nai|effect on intervals}}  {{ind|general-imported|negated intervals|meaning of}} Negated intervals, marked with a 
:{{jbo|-nai}} following the BIhI cmavo, indicate an interval that includes everything but what is between the endpoints (with respect to some understood scale):

{{dsp|example-random-id-39EI}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-39EI}}
{{judri|c14e16d9}}
{{ind|example|except from 10 to 12|example}}
:'''do dicra .e'a mi ca la daucac. bi'onai la gaicac.'''
:<code>You disturb (allowed) me at 10 not-from ... to 12</code>
:''You can contact me except from 10 to 12.''

The complete syntax of joiks is:

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|GAhO selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|JOI selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|nai}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|se}}  {{ind|general-imported|joiks|syntax of}}

*{{grammar|[se] JOI  [nai]}}
*{{grammar|[se] BIhI [nai]}}
*{{grammar|GAhO [se] BIhI [nai] GAhO}}

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|JOI selma'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|joigik|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|intervals|forethought}} Notice that the colloquial English translations of 
{{vla|bi'i}} and 
{{vla|bi'o}} have forethought form: 
“between ... and” for 
{{vla|bi'i}}, and 
“from ... to” for 
{{vla|bi'o}}. In Lojban too, non-logical connectives can be expressed in forethought. Rather than using a separate selma'o, the forethought logical connectives are constructed from the afterthought ones by suffixing {{vla|gi}}. Such a compound cmavo is not unnaturally called a “joigik”; the syntax of joigiks is any of:

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|GAhO selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|JOI selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|BIhI selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|nai}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|se}}  {{ind|general-imported|joigiks|syntax of}}
*{{grammar|[se] JOI  [nai] GI}}
*{{grammar|[se] BIhI [nai] GI}}
*{{grammar|GAhO [se] BIhI [nai] GAhO GI}}

{{ind|general-imported|joigiks|connection types}} Joigiks may be used to non-logically connect bridi, sumti, and bridi-tails; and also in termsets.

{{lex|example-random-id-pC5x}} in forethought becomes:

{{dsp|example-random-id-iBpP}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-iBpP}}
{{judri|c14e16d10}}
{{ind|example|carry the piano|example}}
:'''joigi la djan. gi la .alis. bevri le pipno'''
:<code>[Together] John and Alice carry the piano.</code>

The first 
{{vla|gi}} is part of the joigik; the second {{vla|gi}} is the regular gik that separates the two things being connected in all forethought forms.

{{lex|example-random-id-qGtv}} can be expressed in forethought as:

{{dsp|example-random-id-u51K}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-u51K}}
{{judri|c14e16d11}}
{{ind|example|between Dresden and Frankfurt|example}}
:'''mi ca sanli ke'i bi'i ga'o gi la drezdn. gi la frankfurt.'''
:<code>I [present] stand [exclusive] between [inclusive] Dresden and Frankfurt.</code>
:''I am standing between Dresden (exclusive) and Frankfurt (inclusive).''

{{ind|general-imported|GAhO position in forethought intervals}}  {{ind|general-imported|forethought intervals|GAhO position}} In forethought, unfortunately, the GAhOs become physically separated from the endpoints, but the same rule applies: the first GAhO refers to the first endpoint.

{{ssp|section-mekso-connections}}
==Logical and non-logical connectives within mekso==
{{ind|general-imported|mathematical expressions|connectives in}}  {{ind|general-imported|non-logical connection|in mathematical expressions}}  {{ind|general-imported|logical connection|in mathematical expressions}} Lojban has a separate grammar embedded within the main grammar for representing mathematical expressions (or mekso in Lojban) such as “2 + 2”. Mathematical expressions are explained fully in {{lch|chapter-mekso}}. The basic components of mekso are operands, like 
“2”, and operators, like “+”. Both of these may be either logically or non-logically connected.

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|JOI selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|GUhA selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|JA selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|GA selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|A selma'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|connecting operators|with bo in connective}}  {{ind|general-imported|bo|in joiks for operators}}  {{ind|general-imported|bo|in jeks for operators}}  {{ind|general-imported|guheks|connecting operators}}  {{ind|general-imported|jeks|connecting operators}}  {{ind|general-imported|operators|connecting}}  {{ind|general-imported|operands|connecting}}  {{ind|general-imported|geks|connecting operands}}  {{ind|general-imported|eks|connecting operands}} Operands are connected in afterthought with eks and in forethought with geks, just like sumti. Operators, on the other hand, are connected in afterthought with jeks and in forethought with guheks, just like tanru components. (However, jeks and joiks with 

{{vla|bo}} are not allowed for operators.) This parallelism is no accident.

{{ind|general-imported|operators|analogue of tanru in}}  {{ind|general-imported|connecting operators|with ke in connective}}  {{ind|general-imported|connecting operands|with ke in connective}}  {{ind|general-imported|connecting operands|with bo in connective}} In addition, eks with 
{{vla|bo}} and with 
{{vla|ke}}&hellip;{{vla|ke'e}} are allowed for grouping logically connected operands, and 
{{vla|ke}}&hellip;{{vla|ke'e}} is allowed for grouping logically connected operators, although there is no analogue of tanru among the operators.

Only a few examples of each kind of mekso connection will be given. Despite the large number of rules required to support this feature, it is of relatively minor importance in either the mekso or the logical-connective scheme of things. These examples are drawn from 
{{ls|section-connectives-within-mekso}}, and contain many mekso features not explained in this chapter.

{{lex|example-random-id-gMU4}} exhibits afterthought logical connection between operands:

{{dsp|example-random-id-gMU4}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-gMU4}}
{{judri|c14e17d1}}
{{ind|example|three of four people|example}}
:'''vei ci .a vo [ve'o] prenu cu klama le zarci'''
:<code>( Three or four ) people go-to the market.</code>

{{lex|example-random-id-ftNY}} is equivalent in meaning, but uses forethought connection:

{{dsp|example-random-id-ftNY}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-ftNY}}
{{judri|c14e17d2}}
:'''vei ga ci gi vo [ve'o] prenu cu klama le zarci'''
:<code>( Either 3 or 4 ) people go-to the market.</code>

Note that the mekso in 
{{lex|example-random-id-gMU4}} and 
{{lex|example-random-id-ftNY}} are being used as quantifiers. Lojban requires that any mekso other than a simple number be enclosed in 
{{vla|vei}} and 
{{vla|ve'o}} parentheses when used as a quantifier. The right parenthesis mark, 
{{vla|ve'o}}, is an elidable terminator.

Simple examples of logical connection between operators are hard to come by. A contrived example is:

{{dsp|example-random-id-dCxf}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-dCxf}}
{{judri|c14e17d3}}
:'''li re su'i je pi'i re du li vo'''
:<code>The-number 2 plus and times 2 equals the-number 4.</code>
:''{{math|2 + 2 = 4}} and {{math|2 x 2 = 4}}.''

The forethought form of 
{{lex|example-random-id-dCxf}} is:

{{dsp|example-random-id-YBD6}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-YBD6}}
{{judri|c14e17d4}}
:'''li re ge su'i gi pi'i re du li vo'''
:<code>The-number two both plus and times two equals the-number four.</code>
:''Both {{math|2 + 2 = 4}} and {{math|2 x 2 = 4}}.''

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|ke'i}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|ga'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|mathematical intervals}} Non-logical connection with joiks or joigiks is also permitted between operands and between operators. One use for this construct is to connect operands with 

{{vla|bi'i}} to create mathematical intervals:

{{dsp|example-random-id-z2oF}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-z2oF}}
{{judri|c14e17d5}}
{{ind|example|zero to one|example}}
:'''li no ga'o bi'i ke'i pa'''
:<code>the-number zero (inclusive) from-to (exclusive) one</code>
{{math|[0,1)}}
:''the numbers from zero to one, including zero but not including one''

{{ind|general-imported|compound subscript}} You can also combine two operands with 
{{vla|ce'o}}, the sequence connective of selma'o JOI, to make a compound subscript:

{{dsp|example-random-id-8rEL}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-8rEL}}
{{judri|c14e17d6}}
{{ind|example|x sub b,d|example}} 
:'''xy. boi xi vei by. ce'o dy. [ve'o]'''
:<code>“x” sub ( “b” sequence “d”)</code>
:{{math|x<subscript>b,d</subscript>}}

Note that the 
{{vla|boi}} in 
{{lex|example-random-id-8rEL}} is not elidable, because the 
{{vla|xi}} subscript needs something to attach to.

{{ssp|section-sumtcita}}
==Tenses, modals, and logical connection==
The tense and modal systems of Lojban interact with the logical connective system. No one chapter can explain all of these simultaneously, so each chapter must present its own view of the area of interaction with emphasis on its own concepts and terminology. In the examples of this chapter, the many tenses of various selma'o as well as the modals of selma'o BAI are represented by the simple time cmavo 
{{vla|pu}}, {{vla|ca}}, and {{vla|ba}} (of selma'o PU) representing the past, the present, and the future respectively. Preceding a selbri, these cmavo state the time when the bridi was, is, or will be true (analogous to English verb tenses); preceding a sumti, they state that the event of the main bridi is before, simultaneous with, or after the event given by the sumti (which is generally a {{jbo|le nu}} abstraction; See {{ls|section-events}}).

{{ind|general-imported|logically connected tenses|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|logical connection|interaction with tenses}} The two types of interaction between tenses and logical connectives are logically connected tenses and tensed logical connections. The former are fairly simple. Jeks may be used between tense cmavo to specify two connected bridi that differ only in tense:

{{dsp|example-random-id-g6iT}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-g6iT}}
{{judri|c14e18d1}}
{{ind|example|once and future king|example}}
:'''la .artr. pu nolraitru .ije la .artr. ba nolraitru'''
:<code>Arthur [past] is-a-noblest-governor. And Arthur [future] is-a-noblest-governor.</code>
:''Arthur was a king, and Arthur will be a king.''

can be reduced to:

{{dsp|example-random-id-PLgw}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-PLgw}}
{{judri|c14e18d2}}
{{ind|example|once and future king|example}}
:'''la .artr. pu je ba nolraitru'''
:<code>Arthur [past] and [future] is-a-noblest-governor.</code>
:''Arthur was and will be king.''

{{lex|example-random-id-g6iT}} and 
{{lex|example-random-id-PLgw}} are equivalent in meaning; neither says anything about whether Arthur is king now.

{{ind|general-imported|non-logically connected tenses}} Non-logical connection with joiks is also possible between tenses:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Mcsi}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Mcsi}}
{{judri|c14e18d3}}
{{ind|example|breathe|example}}
:'''mi pu bi'o ba vasxu'''
:<code>I [past] from ... to [future] breathe.</code>
:''I breathe from a past time until a future time.''

The full tense system makes more interesting tense intervals expressible, such as “from a medium time ago until a long time from now”.

{{ind|general-imported|tenses|grouping of connectives in}}  {{ind|general-imported|grouping|of connection in tenses}}  {{ind|general-imported|tenses|forethought connection in}}  {{ind|general-imported|forethought connection|in tenses}} No forethought connections between tenses are permitted by the grammar, nor is there any way to override the default left-grouping rule; these limitations are imposed to keep the tense grammar simpler. Whatever can be said with tenses or modals can be said with subordinate bridi stating the time, place, or mode explicitly, so it is reasonable to try to remove at least some complications.

{{ind|general-imported|tensed logical connection}} Tensed logical connections are both more complex and more important than logical connections between tenses. Consider the English sentence:

{{dsp|example-random-id-efav}}
{{judri|c14e18d4}}
{{ind|example|went and bought|example}}
I went to the market, and I bought food.

The verbatim translation of 
{{lex|example-random-id-efav}}, namely:

{{dsp|example-random-id-PMTu}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-PMTu}}
{{judri|c14e18d5}}
:'''mi pu klama le zarci .ije mi pu tervecnu lo cidja'''
:<code>I [past] go-to the market. And I [past] buy items-of food.</code>

fails to fully represent a feature of the English, namely that the buying came after the going. (It also fails to represent that the buying was a consequence of the going, which can be expressed by a modal that is discussed in 
{{lch|chapter-sumti-tcita}}.) However, the tense information &ndash; that the event of my going to the market preceded the event of my buying food &ndash; can be added to the logical connective as follows. The 
{{vla|.i}}{{vla|je}} is replaced by 
{{vla|.i}}{{vla|je}}{{vla|bo}}, and the tense cmavo 
{{vla|ba}} is inserted between 
{{vla|.i}}{{vla|je}} and 
{{vla|bo}}:

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|.ijebabo}}

{{dsp|example-random-id-BPG1}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-BPG1}}
{{judri|c14e18d6}}
:'''mi pu klama le zarci .ijebabo mi pu tervecnu lo cidja'''
:<code>I [past] go-to the market. And [later] I [past] buy items-of food.</code>

Here the 
{{vla|pu}} cmavo in the two bridi-tails express the time of both actions with respect to the speaker: in the past. The 
{{vla|ba}} relates the two items to one another: the second item is later than the first item. The grammar does not permit omitting the 
{{vla|bo}}; if it were omitted, the 
{{vla|ba}} and the second 
{{vla|pu}} would run together to form a compound tense 

{{vla|bapu}} applying to the second bridi-tail only.

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|A selma'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|tensed logical connectives|in ek…bo}} Adding tense or modal information to a logical connective is permitted only in the following situations:

Between an ek (or joik) and 
{{vla|bo}}, as in:

{{dsp|example-random-id-129L}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-129L}}
{{judri|c14e18d7}}
{{ind|example|simultaneously|example}}
:'''la .djan .ecabo la .alis. klama le zarci'''
:<code>John and [simultaneous] Alice go-to the market.</code>
:''John and Alice go to the market simultaneously.''

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|JOI selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|A selma'o}}  

{{ind|general-imported|tensed logical connectives|in joik…ke}}  {{ind|general-imported|tensed logical connectives|in ek…ke}} Between an ek (or joik) and 
{{vla|ke}}, as in:

{{dsp|example-random-id-nydK}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-nydK}}
{{judri|c14e18d8}}
{{ind|example|and earlier|example}}
:'''mi dzukla le zarci .epuke le zdani .a le ckule [ke'e]'''
:<code>I walk-to the market and [earlier] ( the house or the school ).</code>
:''I walk to the market and, before that, to the house or the school.''

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|GIhA selma'o}}  

{{ind|general-imported|tensed logical connectives|in gihek…bo}} Between a gihek and 
{{vla|bo}}, as in:

{{dsp|example-random-id-APPE}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-APPE}}
{{ind|example|and then}}  
{{judri|c14e18d9}}
:'''mi dunda le cukta gi'ebabo lebna lo rupnu vau do'''
:<code>I give the book and [later] take some currency-units from/to you.</code>
:''I give you the book and then take some dollars (pounds, yen) from you.''

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|GIhA selma'o}}  
{{ind|general-imported|tensed logical connectives|in gihek…ke}} Between a gihek and 
{{vla|ke}}, as in:

{{dsp|example-random-id-A0yC}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-A0yC}}
{{judri|c14e18d10}}
{{ind|example|and simultaneously|example}}
:'''mi dzukla le zarci gi'ecake cusku zo'e la djan. [ke'e]'''
:<code>I walk-to the market and [simultaneous] express something to-John.</code>
:''I walk to the market and at the same time talk to John.''

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|I selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|JA selma'o}}  

{{ind|general-imported|tensed logical connectives|in ijoik…bo}}  {{ind|general-imported|tensed logical connectives|in ijek…bo}} Between an ijek (or ijoik) and {{vla|bo}}, as in:

{{dsp|example-random-id-AhnP}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-AhnP}}
{{judri|c14e18d11}}
{{ind|example|and then|example}}
:'''mi viska pa nanmu .ijebabo mi viska pa ninmu'''
:<code>I see a man. And [later] I see a woman.</code>
:''I see a man, and then I see a woman.''

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|I selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|JOI selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|JA selma'o}}  

{ind|general-imported|tensed logical connectives|in ijoik…tu'e}}  {{ind|general-imported|tensed logical connectives|in ijek…tu'e}} Between an ijek (or ijoik) and {{vla|tu'e}}, as in:

{{dsp|example-random-id-GBgP}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-GBgP}}
{{judri|c14e18d12}}
{{ind|example|and then|example}}
:'''mi viska pa nanmu .ijebatu'e mi viska pa ninmu [tu'u]'''
:<code>I see a man. And [later] I see a woman.</code>
:''I see a man, and then I see a woman.''

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|JA selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|JOI selma'o}}  

{{ind|general-imported|tensed logical connectives|in joik…bo}}  {{ind|general-imported|tensed logical connectives|in jek…bo}} And finally, between a jek (or joik) and 
{{vla|bo}}, as in:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Ce09}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Ce09}}
{{judri|c14e18d13}}
{{ind|example|doctor and then rich|example}}
:'''mi mikce jebabo ricfu'''
:<code>I-am-a doctor and [later] rich</code>
:''I am a doctor and future rich person.''

{{ind|general-imported|tu'e|contrasted with bo for tensed logical connection}}  {{ind|general-imported|bo|contrasted with tu'e for tensed logical connection}}  {{ind|general-imported|ke|contrasted with bo for tensed logical connection}}  {{ind|general-imported|bo|contrasted with ke for tensed logical connection}} As can be seen from 
{{lex|example-random-id-AhnP}} and 
{{lex|example-random-id-GBgP}}, the choice between 
{{vla|bo}} and {{vla|ke}} (or {{vla|tu'e}}) is arbitrary when there are only two things to be connected. If there were no tense information to include, of course neither would be required; it is only the rule that tense information must always be sandwiched between the logical connective and a following {{vla|bo}}, 
{{vla|ke}}, or {{vla|tu'e}} that requires the use of one of these grouping cmavo in {{lex|example-random-id-129L}} and {{lex|example-random-id-APPE}} through 
{{lex|example-random-id-Ce09}}.

{{ind|general-imported|mathematical expressions|tensed connection in}}  {{ind|general-imported|tensed connectives|in mathematical expressions}}  {{ind|general-imported|tensed non-logical connectives|forethought}}  {{ind|general-imported|tensed logical connectives|forethought}}  {{ind|general-imported|forethought connectives|with tense}}  {{ind|general-imported|tensed non-logical connectives}}  {{ind|general-imported|non-logical connectives|including tense}} Non-logical connectives with 
{{vla|bo}} and 
{{vla|ke}} can include tense information in exactly the same way as logical connectives. Forethought connectives, however (except as noted below) are unable to do so, as are termsets or tense connectives. Mathematical operands and operators can also include tense information in their logical connectives as a result of their close parallelism with sumti and tanru components respectively:

{{dsp|example-random-id-sgUo}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-sgUo}}
{{judri|c14e18d14}}
:'''vei ci .ebabo vo [ve'o] tadni cu zvati le kumfa'''
:<code>( 3 and [future] 4 ) students are-at the room.</code>
:''Three and, later, four students were in the room.''

{{ind|general-imported|forethought bridi-tail connection|special rule for tense}}  {{ind|general-imported|tense|in forethought bridi-tail connection|special rule}} is a simple example. There is a special grammatical rule for use when a tense applies to both of the selbri in a forethought bridi-tail connection: the entire forethought construction can just be preceded by a tense. For example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-DxuA}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-DxuA}}
{{judri|c14e18d15}}
{{ind|example|went and bought|example}}
:'''mi pu ge klama le zarci gi tervecnu lo cidja'''
:<code>I [past] both go-to the market and buy some food</code>
:''I went to the market and bought some food.''

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|pu ge}}  

{{lex|example-random-id-DxuA}} is similar to 
{{lex|example-random-id-PMTu}}. There is no time relationship specified between the going and the buying; both are simply set in the past.

{{ssp|section-abstractors}}
==Abstractor connection and connection within abstractions==
{{ind|lojban-word-imported|JA selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|NU selma'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|jeks|connecting abstractors}}  {{ind|general-imported|abstractions|logical connection of}}  {{ind|general-imported|logical connection of abstractors}} Last and (as a matter of fact) least: a logical connective is allowed between abstraction markers of selma'o NU. As usual, the connection can be expanded to a bridi connection between two bridi which differ only in abstraction marker. Jeks are the appropriate connective. 

{{lex|example-random-id-qGVP}} and 
{{lex|example-random-id-qgVR}} are equivalent in meaning:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qGVP}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qGVP}}
{{judri|c14e19d1}}
{{ind|example|quality and quantity|example}}
:'''le ka la frank. ciska cu xlali .ije le ni la frank. ciska cu xlali'''
:<code>The quality-of Frank's writing is bad, and the quantity of Frank's writing is bad.</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qgVR}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qgVR}}
{{judri|c14e19d2}}
{{ind|example|quality and quantity|example}}
:'''le ka je ni la frank. ciska cu xlali'''
:''The quality and quantity of Frank's writing is bad.''

{{ind|general-imported|abstractions|grouping of connectives in}}  {{ind|general-imported|grouping|of connection in abstractions}}  {{ind|general-imported|abstractions|forethought connection in}}  {{ind|general-imported|forethought connection|in abstractions}} As with tenses and modals, there is no forethought and no way to override the left-grouping rule.

{{ind|general-imported|logical connection|inside abstractions|contrasted with outside}}  {{ind|general-imported|logical connection|in abstractions|inner bridi contrasted with outer bridi}} Logical connectives and abstraction are related in another way as well, though. Since an abstraction contains a bridi, the bridi may have a logical connection inside it. Is it legitimate to split the outer bridi into two, joined by the logical connection? Absolutely not. For example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-f1uT}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-f1uT}}
{{judri|c14e19d3}}
{{ind|example|Jupiter life|example}}
:'''mi jinvi le du'u loi jmive cu zvati gi'onai na zvati vau la .iupiter.'''
:<code>I opine the fact-that a-mass-of living-things (is-at or-else isn't-at) Jupiter.</code>
:''I believe there either is or isn't life on Jupiter.''

is true, since the embedded sentence is a tautology, but:

{{dsp|example-random-id-X69J}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-X69J}}
{{judri|c14e19d4}}
:'''mi jinvi le du'u loi jmive cu zvati la .iupiter. .ijonai mi jinvi le du'u loi jmive cu zvati la .iupiter.'''
:<code>I opine the fact-that a-mass-of living-things is-at Jupiter or-else I opine the fact-that a-mass-of living-things isn't-at Jupiter</code>

is false, since I have no evidence one way or the other ( 
{{vla|jinvi}} requires some sort of evidence, real or fancied, unlike 
{{vla|krici}}).

(Other compound cmavo are often possible: for example, 
{{vla|se}}{{vla|.a}} means the same as 
{{vla|a}}, and could be used instead.)

<tab class=wikitable header=true>
truth	ek	jek	gihek	gek-gik	guhek-gik

TTFT	{{vla|.a}}{{vla|nai}}	{{vla|ja}}{{vla|nai}}	{{vla|gi'a}}{{vla|nai}}	{{vla|ga}}-{{vla|gi}}{{vla|nai}}	{{vla|gu'a}}-{{vla|gi}}{{vla|nai}}

Note: ijeks are exactly the same as the corresponding jeks, except for the prefixed
{{vla|i}}.

{{ssp|section-construction-summary}}
==Rules for making logical and non-logical connectives==
{{ind|general-imported|non-logical connectives|syntax rules summary}}  {{ind|general-imported|logical connectives|syntax rules summary}} The full set of rules for inserting 
{{vla|na}}, 
{{vla|se}}, and 
{{vla|nai}} into any connective is:

Afterthought logical connectives (eks, jeks, giheks, ijeks):
*Negate first construct: Place {{vla|na}} before the connective cmavo (but after the {{vla|i}} of an ijek).
*Negate second construct: Place {{vla|nai}} after the connective cmavo.
*Exchange constructs: Place {{vla|se}} before the connective cmavo (after {{vla|na}} if any).

Forethought logical connectives (geks, guheks):
*Negate first construct: Place 
{{vla|nai}} after the connective cmavo.
*Negate second construct: Place 
{{vla|nai}} after the 
{{vla|gi}}.
*Exchange constructs: Place 
{{vla|se}} before the connective cmavo.

Non-logical connectives (joiks, joigiks):
*Negate connection: Place 
{{vla|nai}} after the connective cmavo (but before the 
{{vla|gi}} of a joigik).
*Exchange constructs: Place 
{{vla|se}} before the connective cmavo.
